notes.title: Count True Values in Ranges
notes.takeaway: “does this range contain any true?” into “is this range’s count of true values greater than zero?”
notes.details: For a Boolean range, existence is equivalent to a positive count of true entries. A prefix- or suffix-count difference can answer that question without scanning the range.

notes.title: Optimize the Transition Lookup
notes.takeaway: Sometimes the DP state is already good—the expensive part is how we look up its transitions.
notes.details: A correct DP state need not change merely because its implementation is slow. Check whether repeatedly searching its candidate transitions is the expensive part before redesigning the state.

notes.title: Minimum Tail for Each Length
notes.takeaway: Instead of asking for the longest sequence ending at each index, ask for the smallest ending value achievable at each length.
notes.details: For increasing subsequences, tails[i] records the smallest ending value found for length i + 1. This changes what the state represents; it is not just a compressed version of the longest-subsequence-ending-at-index DP.

notes.title: Farthest Reach by Refuel Count
notes.takeaway: When farther progress dominates, turn 'minimum actions to reach the target' into 'farthest progress possible with k actions'; find the first k that reaches the target.
notes.details: For refueling stops, retain the farthest distance reachable with exactly k refuels, since farther reach dominates at the same count. Process each station's count updates backward to use it once, then take the first count that reaches the target.

notes.title: Count Pairs by Exact GCD
notes.takeaway: Instead of computing the GCD of every pair, count how many pairs have each possible GCD.
notes.details: Count values divisible by each d to obtain pairs whose GCD is a multiple of d. Processing d downward and subtracting counts for larger multiples yields exact GCD counts; cumulative counts then support kth-pair queries.

notes.title: Fix the Path Ending Node
notes.takeaway: Instead of fixing a start and searching for endings, fix an ending and count the starts that work.
notes.details: For downward target-sum paths, consider each node as the endpoint and count compatible starting positions on its ancestor chain. This reverses the viewpoint of launching a fresh endpoint search from every possible start.

notes.title: Count Each Node's Path Contribution
notes.takeaway: Sum each whole path—or let each node contribute its value times the number of paths containing it.
notes.details: The total over root-to-leaf path sums can be computed by adding completed path sums at leaves. Equivalently, each node contributes its value multiplied by the number of those paths containing it.

notes.title: Enumerate the Smaller Digit Sum
notes.takeaway: Guess the small unknown and derive the large one. The first number may have 100,000 digits, but its digit sum is small and fixes the rest of the chain.
notes.details: In a chain of repeated digit sums, choosing the second number determines the entire remaining tail, even when the first number has up to 100,000 digits. Check the tail against the available digit counts and require the leftover digits to sum to the chosen second number.

notes.title: Required Health on Cell Entry
notes.takeaway: A path's final sum cannot tell you whether you survived every earlier cell. Store the health needed on entry, and work backward.
notes.details: Dungeon survival requires health to stay at least one at every cell, so a final path sum loses essential information. Work backward with the minimum entry health: subtract the current cell from the better right/down requirement, then clamp the result to at least one.

notes.title: Pair Each Sale With Earlier Minimum
notes.takeaway: Fix the selling day: every legal trade has one, and its best partner is the cheapest earlier buying day.
notes.details: For a single stock trade, the best purchase paired with a selling day is the cheapest legal earlier day. Considering every selling day covers every possible optimal trade.

notes.title: Search Only the Smaller Partition
notes.takeaway: Choose the smaller side of a partition to remove the absolute value: minimizing |S−2s| becomes maximizing reachable s at or below S/2.
notes.details: For a partition with total sum S, name the smaller side s so that s is at most floor(S/2). The difference is then S - 2s, so minimizing it means finding the largest reachable s in that range.

notes.title: Triangle Continuations Simplify the Boundary
notes.takeaway: Reverse a path-DP question when it simplifies the boundary: in a triangle, 'best continuation from here' has two valid children at every nonterminal cell and one fixed answer at the apex.
notes.details: Define a triangle state as the best continuation from the current cell to the bottom. Every nonterminal cell has two valid children and the answer is at the apex; this simplifies boundaries without changing the asymptotic complexity of the alternative forward state.

notes.title: Burn Time Is Minimized at Centers
notes.takeaway: The fastest burn start is the node minimizing its farthest distance—the center, not necessarily the root.
notes.details: When burning spreads across one edge per unit time, a starting node's completion time is its farthest distance to any node. Choosing the fastest start therefore means finding a tree center, which need not be the designated root.

notes.title: Farthest Distance From the Infection Start
notes.takeaway: Infection time is the farthest edge distance from the fixed start—not the tree’s diameter.
notes.details: With infection starting at minute zero and crossing one edge per minute, completion time is the maximum distance from that fixed start. The tree diameter can have different endpoints and is not generally the required answer.

notes.title: Align Ancestor Chains Before Walking
notes.takeaway: Parent pointers turn LCA into linked-list intersection: ancestor chains share a suffix, so align their lengths before walking together.
notes.details: With parent pointers, first raise the deeper node until both nodes have the same depth. Moving both upward together then reaches their lowest common ancestor simultaneously, just as aligned linked lists meet at their shared suffix.

notes.title: Leaf Removal Rounds Equal Subtree Height
notes.takeaway: Repeated leaf-removal rounds are subtree heights: a parent waits for its slower child branch, then disappears one round later.
notes.details: Use round zero for leaves and -1 for a null child. A node's removal round is one plus the larger child round because every child must disappear first; this is height in edges, not depth or distance to the nearest leaf.

notes.title: Initialize Capacity and Exact Weight Differently
notes.takeaway: Initialization follows the question a state answers: the empty selection fits every at-most capacity, but reaches only exact weight zero.
notes.details: For maximum value within an at-most capacity, the empty selection gives value zero at every initial capacity. For exact weight, only weight zero is initially reachable; positive weights need an unreachable sentinel rather than zero.

notes.title: Take and Skip Are Transitions
notes.takeaway: Take and skip are choices used to calculate a state; they do not automatically require separate state dimensions.
notes.details: In standard 0/1 knapsack, taking or skipping an item are alternatives used to calculate an item-and-capacity state. Those choices do not by themselves require separate included and excluded state arrays.

notes.title: Charge Cash Only on Stock Trades
notes.takeaway: Holding is a state; buying is a transition. Charge the price when entering the state, not every day spent in it.
notes.details: A holding state describes whether a share is owned, while buying and selling are actions that change cash. Subtract the price only when buying and add it only when selling; merely remaining in either state does not change the balance.

notes.title: Cash Balance Encodes the Purchase Cost
notes.takeaway: A cash-balance state already contains the purchase cost; remembering the purchase day or price separately adds no information.
notes.details: In the stock-trading cash-balance state, buying already subtracts the purchase price. For this formulation, retaining that price or purchase day separately adds no information needed by future transitions.

notes.title: Transaction Allowance Versus Exact Count
notes.takeaway: A count dimension can mean an allowance, not an exact count; aggregating 'at most k' histories can remove a final maximum over exact-count buckets.
notes.details: An at-most-k transaction state includes histories using fewer than k transactions. With consistent transitions and initialization, its final nonholding value already covers zero through k trades, avoiding a separate maximum over exact-count states.

notes.title: Separate Count Meaning From Accounting Action
notes.takeaway: Which histories a state aggregates and which action changes its counter are separate design choices.
notes.details: Exact versus at-most defines which trading histories a state combines. Whether the transaction counter changes on buying or selling is a separate choice; the recurrence and base cases must consistently follow both decisions.

notes.title: Memo Keys Must Preserve Remaining Choices
notes.takeaway: Two calls may share a memo key only if they describe the same remaining subproblem—not merely the same remaining amount.
notes.details: For unlimited coin change, remaining amount alone can identify the subproblem when every denomination remains available. If items are usable only once, identical amounts may still have different remaining choices, so the memo key must preserve that distinction.

notes.title: Item Layers Survive Storage Compression
notes.takeaway: We removed the item dimension from storage, not from the algorithm's logic.
notes.details: In coin-outer tabulation, the outer loop still determines which denominations have been processed. Using one amount array removes the stored item dimension, not its role in the recurrence or update order.

notes.title: Merge Counters With a Proven Invariant
notes.takeaway: Two equal counters that must move in lockstep are one state variable, not two.
notes.details: For a still-valid Good Schedule segment, the two viewers have watched identical sets because earlier days selected the same episode for both or nothing for both. Their needed counters therefore remain equal and can be represented by one variable; the reduction depends on that invariant.

notes.title: Separate Floyd Endpoints From Allowed Intermediates
notes.takeaway: In reverse-deletion Floyd DP, inactive vertices may remain endpoints of stored distances; only allowed intermediates constrain the path, while active endpoints constrain the reported sum.
notes.details: In reverse-deletion Floyd DP, added vertices restrict intermediate path vertices, not the endpoints whose distances are stored. Update all endpoint pairs at each layer, and use active status only when summing distances between currently active endpoints.

notes.title: Substring States End at Current Characters
notes.takeaway: A common-substring state ends exactly at both current characters; on a mismatch it resets, unlike an LCS state that is best anywhere in the prefixes.
notes.details: A common-substring state measures a contiguous match ending at both current characters. A mismatch resets it to zero; copying from the top or left would import a match that does not satisfy that endpoint contract.

notes.title: Handled Endpoints Leave the Remaining Subproblem
notes.takeaway: Removing an endpoint from the remaining subproblem does not necessarily delete it from the solution; it may already be handled by an inserted partner.
notes.details: In minimum insertions for a palindrome, excluding an endpoint from the recursive interval does not mean deleting it. The extra insertion supplies its matching partner, so that endpoint is already handled while the smaller interval is solved.

notes.title: Boundary Reachability Carries Past Obstacles
notes.takeaway: A free cell is not necessarily reachable; along a grid boundary, copying the previous path count carries earlier blockages forward.
notes.details: Along a grid's first row or first column, a free cell beyond an obstacle still has no path from the start. Copying the preceding path count propagates that zero reachability without treating every free boundary cell as reachable.

notes.title: Remember the Last String's Chosen Form
notes.takeaway: If the next transition depends on whether the last string was reversed, the state must remember that final form—not just the best cost so far.
notes.details: When strings may be reversed to obtain a nondecreasing lexicographic sequence, future comparisons depend on the last string's selected form. Keep separate minimum costs for original and reversed forms, and mark impossible states as unreachable rather than zero-cost.

notes.title: Zeros Turn Fixed Sums Into Ranges
notes.takeaway: If a zero can become any positive integer, an array with a zero can realize every sum from its minimum upward; without a zero, its sum is fixed.
notes.details: Replacing each zero with a positive integer gives a minimum sum of the existing sum plus the zero count. An array containing a zero can reach every larger sum; an array without zeros has a fixed sum, which must fall within the other array's achievable range.

notes.title: Preserve Unmatched Brackets for Segment Merges
notes.takeaway: A segment summary must retain what can interact across its boundary. For brackets, matched pairs alone are not enough; unmatched opens and closes are needed to merge.
notes.details: A bracket segment needs its matched-pair count plus unmatched opens and closes. Merging adjacent segments can pair left-side unmatched opens with right-side unmatched closes, so returning only the matched count from a partial query loses necessary boundary information.

notes.title: Return Height or an Imbalance Sentinel
notes.takeaway: Return the useful result on success and an impossible result as failure; one bottom-up pass can carry both.
notes.details: A balanced-tree helper can return its subtree height on success and -1 when an imbalance is found. Because valid heights are nonnegative, the sentinel carries failure without a separate Boolean or repeated height computations.

notes.title: Subtree Size Differs From Removal Score
notes.takeaway: The value returned to your parent and the answer computed at your node may describe different situations.
notes.details: Removing a node excludes that node from its score's components, but its parent still needs the size of the intact subtree. A leaf therefore returns size one upward even though its own removal leaves a component of size n - 1 when that component exists.

notes.title: Global Existence Does Not Imply Local Presence
notes.takeaway: A target can be guaranteed to exist globally and still be absent from the subtree this call is searching.
notes.details: A target guaranteed to occur somewhere in the tree may be absent from the subtree of a particular recursive call. The helper still needs a result that distinguishes local absence from a successful search.

notes.title: Store Frequency Parity for Palindrome Paths
notes.takeaway: If the answer only depends on odd versus even counts, store parity—not the full frequencies.
notes.details: For pseudo-palindromic paths, the relevant property of each value's count is whether it is odd or even. Retaining exact frequencies stores more information than the path-validity check needs.

notes.title: Reset a Chain Without Pruning Descendants
notes.takeaway: A mismatch prevents extension, not traversal.
notes.details: In a consecutive parent-to-child path search, a child value that breaks the current chain cannot extend it. Its subtree must still be traversed because a new valid chain may begin at that child or farther below.

notes.title: Specify Which End the Path State Anchors
notes.takeaway: Top-down tracks a path ending here; bottom-up returns a path starting here.
notes.details: For consecutive parent-to-child paths, a top-down state describes a chain ending at the current node, while a bottom-up return describes one starting there. Both can visit each node once with O(h) recursion space; choosing a return contract changes the interface, not the asymptotic complexity.

notes.title: Track the Marginal Cost of Pushing Increments
notes.takeaway: A corrected value tells you how much is missing; a marginal push cost tells you where to send it.
notes.details: In the minimum-total-increments children-sum variant, corrected child values determine the missing amount but not where to send it. Track the extra cost of increasing each subtree root by one: propagation through the cheapest existing child gives one plus that child's push cost.

notes.title: Preorder Consumption Encodes the Lower Constraint
notes.takeaway: A shared preorder index is not just bookkeeping: it records that earlier subtree regions have been completely consumed.
notes.details: For a guaranteed-valid BST preorder with distinct values, a shared advancing index ensures earlier subtree regions are consumed before the next region begins. This makes an upper-bound-only construction possible; arbitrary-input validation still needs lower-bound checks and verification that all input was consumed.

notes.title: Root Detection Needs Only Child Membership
notes.takeaway: We do not need to remember who the parent is—only whether a parent exists.
notes.details: For valid parent-child descriptions, finding the root requires knowing which nodes appear as children, not remembering each child's parent. A child-membership set expresses that requirement directly; replacing a Boolean map with it is a semantic simplification, not an asymptotic improvement.

notes.title: Robbery Exclusion Applies to Edges
notes.takeaway: A parent–child exclusion is an edge constraint, not an alternating-level constraint.
notes.details: House Robber III forbids selecting directly connected parent-child pairs, not all nodes on adjacent levels. Restricting the answer to either alternating-level sum misses legal choices such as the two endpoints of the chain 10 → 1 → 1 → 10.

notes.title: Add Independent Best Choices From Both Branches
notes.takeaway: Independent branches contribute a sum of their best choices—not one maximum across all choices.
notes.details: When the current node is not robbed, choose the better allowed result independently in each child subtree and add those results. Taking one maximum across both branches incorrectly discards a contribution, since siblings are not directly connected by the exclusion rule.

notes.title: Judge Candidate BST Subtrees Independently
notes.takeaway: An ancestor outside a candidate subtree must not disqualify that subtree.
notes.details: A candidate BST subtree need not obey value bounds imposed by ancestors outside that subtree. Return local validity, size, and extrema upward, and continue exploring below invalid ancestors so a valid descendant subtree is not rejected prematurely.

notes.title: Combine Sums and Counts Before Averaging
notes.takeaway: To combine averages, return their ingredients—sum and count—not just the averages.
notes.details: Child subtrees can have different sizes, so taking an unweighted average of their averages is incorrect. Return each subtree's sum and count, combine those quantities, and calculate the resulting average from the combined totals.

notes.title: Keep Ancestor Differences on One Chain
notes.takeaway: Max minus min is a valid ancestor difference on one path, but not across a branching subtree: its extremes may be siblings.
notes.details: A root-to-node path's maximum and minimum belong to the same ancestor chain, so their difference is a legal ancestor-descendant difference. Extrema taken across a branching subtree may instead be siblings; root 5 with children 1 and 9 has maximum legal difference 4, not 8.

notes.title: Distinct Paths Need Compatibility Information
notes.takeaway: The best child sum is not enough when branches must also be compatible; you must know what values the chosen paths consume.
notes.details: For a path requiring distinct values, individually best child arms may share a value and be incompatible. A best sum alone loses the values consumed, and memoizing only by node is invalid when different used-value sets change the legal continuations.

notes.title: Allow the Empty BST When Initializing
notes.takeaway: Before seeding a maximum with negative infinity, check whether choosing nothing is a valid zero-valued answer.
notes.details: Maximum Sum BST permits choosing an empty BST with sum zero. Initialize the best answer to zero so all-negative inputs do not force a negative result; a null child also contributes a valid empty subtree with sum zero.

notes.title: Represent an Absent Previous Value Explicitly
notes.takeaway: “No previous value” is a state, not necessarily a special numeric value.
notes.details: INT_MIN is a legal node value, so using it as the previous inorder value can wrongly reject the first node. Use an explicit absent previous node or a genuinely wider sentinel; exclusive BST bounds must likewise lie outside the allowed node-value range.

notes.title: Lexicographic Order Can Reverse After Appending
notes.takeaway: Before keeping only the locally best partial answer, check whether it stays best after future extensions: a < ab, but az > abz.
notes.details: Keeping only the smallest unfinished leaf-to-node string is unsafe when later ancestors append a suffix. Prefix-related candidates can reverse order: a is smaller than ab, but az is larger than abz, so compare complete candidates or retain enough information to avoid discarding a future winner.

notes.title: BST Shape Counts Depend Only on Size
notes.takeaway: To count BST shapes on distinct sorted values, only the number of values matters—not the labels or interval endpoints.
notes.details: For distinct sorted values, relabeling preserves the possible BST shapes, so the count needs only the number of values. Splitting around each possible root multiplies independent left and right counts; an empty side contributes one valid choice.

notes.title: Precompute the Predicate Behind the Count
notes.takeaway: DP can precompute an expensive predicate instead of the final answer.
notes.details: A DP table can store reusable answers to an expensive condition rather than directly store the final count. In a counting problem, this separates checking candidate validity from accumulating valid candidates.

notes.title: Update Only the Changed DP Entries
notes.takeaway: A large DP layer can still have a cheap update: identify which entries actually change when one input element is introduced.
notes.details: In the Good Schedule transition from column L + 1 to L, only the entries indexed by a_L and b_L change. Sweep backward with one array and update those affected entries instead of rebuilding the entire layer.

notes.title: Memoization Still Pays Each State's Transition Cost
notes.takeaway: Memoization removes repeated state computation, not the work inside each state.
notes.details: Caching a state avoids solving that same state repeatedly. Its first evaluation still pays for all internal transition work, so counting memoized states alone does not establish the running time.

notes.title: Generate Only Legal String Predecessors
notes.takeaway: When a state has few possible predecessors, generate them directly instead of testing every earlier candidate.
notes.details: A predecessor in a string chain is obtained by deleting one character from the current word. Generate those candidates and check which exist in the input, rather than comparing the word with every earlier word.

notes.title: Query Compatible Values Through Complement Submasks
notes.takeaway: 'Shares no set bits with x' means 'is a submask of x's complement'; precompute the best value over each mask's submasks.
notes.details: For nonnegative values fitting a chosen finite bit width, y has no set bits in common with x exactly when y is a submask of fullMask XOR x. Precompute the largest input value contained in each mask so the best compatible value can be looked up directly.

notes.title: Enforce Index Order Before Querying Value Order
notes.takeaway: Process states in original index order to enforce 'earlier'; index the aggregate by value to query 'smaller'. The two constraints need not be handled by the same loop.
notes.details: For counting longest increasing subsequences, process elements in their original order so only earlier indices have been inserted. Querying the aggregate over strictly smaller value ranks then enforces the increasing-value condition separately from the index condition.

notes.title: Replace Repeated DP Scans With Range Queries
notes.takeaway: A DP scan over an ordered range can become a range query when its answers have an efficiently mergeable summary; the state itself can stay unchanged.
notes.details: If a DP transition repeatedly combines previous states in an ordered range, look for an efficiently mergeable summary. A range-query structure can replace that scan while leaving the meaning of the DP state unchanged.

notes.title: Shift Reachable Sums From the Previous Bitset
notes.takeaway: A bitset shift adds x to every old reachable sum at once; OR merges take with skip while preserving the same previous-state recurrence.
notes.details: For a nonnegative subset-sum item x, shifting the old reachability bitset by x represents adding that item to every previously reachable sum. OR merges take and skip; the shifted side must come from the pre-update bitset so the same item is not repeatedly reused.

notes.title: Count Singleton Capacity Between Repeated Blocks
notes.takeaway: Separate what is always usable from what consumes a scarce capacity; then count the capacity instead of constructing every placement.
notes.details: In the circle arrangement where every three consecutive cards must contain an equal pair, values with frequency at least two provide usable blocks, while singleton values need supported gaps. Count how many singleton placements those blocks can host, accounting for whether there is one wrapping block or multiple bounded blocks, and require a circle of at least three cards.

notes.title: Count Threshold Violations With Prefix Sums
notes.takeaway: A prefix sum can count a predicate. 'Is there a value greater than v in this rectangle?' becomes 'Is the count of values greater than v nonzero?'
notes.details: When values are bounded by a small V, build a two-dimensional prefix-count grid for each predicate value > v. A candidate's neighborhood has no larger value exactly when the queried count is zero, after handling clipped bounds and the problem's excluded corners.

notes.title: Compress Whole-Block Trades Into Runs
notes.takeaway: When an operation acts on whole equal-character blocks, compress the string into runs and work on run lengths.
notes.details: For a binary-string trade on whole runs, a 0|1|0 pattern's gain is determined by the two neighboring zero-run lengths. Run compression exposes those quantities directly; query-boundary candidates still need their zero runs clipped to the requested interval.

notes.title: Replace a Later-Prefix Search With Suffix Maxima
notes.takeaway: 'Is any eligible later prefix balance at least B[p]?' becomes 'Is the suffix maximum over those eligible positions at least B[p]?'
notes.details: After expressing a segment condition as B[q] >= B[p], a suffix maximum can test whether a qualifying later cut q exists. Its range must include only eligible cuts and preserve a nonempty third segment; the first-cut condition remains a separate check.

notes.title: Count Tied Prefix Maxima Instead of Removals
notes.takeaway: To count repeated removals of the rightmost maximum and everything after it, count the positions that will be chosen: the prefix maxima, including ties.
notes.details: Repeatedly removing the rightmost maximum and everything after it selects exactly those positions at least as large as every earlier element. Count the first element and every later non-strict prefix maximum; tied maxima count separately, so the comparison is >= rather than >.

notes.title: Keep Only the Running Prefix Maximum
notes.takeaway: If future steps only need the running aggregate, keep the aggregate—not the entire prefix history.
notes.details: When counting selected positions in Right Maximum, each next decision needs only the maximum seen so far. A single running maximum replaces the stored prefix-max array because no later step needs an older prefix value.

notes.title: Preprocess BST Values for Repeated Queries
notes.takeaway: After recognizing a familiar single-query task, check whether it repeats; many queries can justify preprocessing once.
notes.details: An inorder traversal already produces sorted BST values, so collect them once and binary-search each closest-node query. This gives O(n + q log n) time regardless of tree shape, but preprocessing is not automatically better for one query or a guaranteed-balanced tree.

notes.title: Find All Preorder Boundaries in One Pass
notes.takeaway: Finding each boundary separately may be quadratic; finding all boundaries together can be linear.
notes.details: Repeatedly scanning for the next greater value can revisit elements and become quadratic. A decreasing monotonic stack computes all next-greater positions in linear time because each index is pushed once and popped at most once; shared-index BST construction can avoid explicit splits altogether.

notes.title: Report a Duplicate at Its Second Occurrence
notes.takeaway: Report a duplicate exactly when its count becomes two; later occurrences need no separate deduplication.
notes.details: When counting occurrences of each subtree representation, add a representative exactly when its frequency reaches two. Later occurrences add nothing, which avoids a separate deduplication set or a second pass solely to identify duplicates.

notes.title: Update Maximum Frequency at the Changed Entry
notes.takeaway: When counts only increase and one entry changes at a time, only that changed entry can raise the running maximum.
notes.details: During subtree-sum counting, only the frequency just incremented can exceed the previous maximum. Update the running maximum immediately, then use one final map scan to collect all sums tied at that frequency.

notes.title: Propagate Batched Subtree-Flip Parity Once
notes.takeaway: Batch subtree flips at their roots, then carry their combined parity down once instead of replaying every update.
notes.details: When all subtree-flip queries are known and only the final state matters, count requests at their roots instead of traversing a subtree for every query. A single downward traversal accumulates ancestor requests modulo two; for initially zero-valued nodes, that parity is the final value.

notes.title: Separate Readiness Scheduling From Child Aggregates
notes.takeaway: The queue decides when a node is ready; the arrays remember what its finished children have already contributed.
notes.details: In bottom-up queue processing, the queue determines when a node's required child results are complete. Arrays can retain partial parent aggregates while another child is pending, so every node's final removal score need not be stored.

notes.title: Subtract the Sibling Group From Its Level
notes.takeaway: Sum the whole level, then subtract the sibling group: cousins are the complement of one local group.
notes.details: Nodes at the same depth are cousins except for those sharing a parent. For each child, subtract its original sibling-group sum from the original next-level total; all children of that parent receive the same replacement value.

notes.title: Layer Order Does Not Guarantee In-Place Safety
notes.takeaway: A valid order between DP layers does not guarantee a safe in-place order inside a layer; dependencies in both directions may still need separate buffers.
notes.details: Cherry Pickup II has a valid bottom-up row order, but each column-pair state reads neighboring pairs in both directions from the next row. Overwriting one shared layer can destroy still-needed values, so row ordering alone does not justify in-place updates.

notes.title: Amount Direction Determines Current-Coin Reuse
notes.takeaway: For coin-outer in-place DP, forward amounts read states that may already use this coin; backward amounts read the previous-item layer.
notes.details: With coins in the outer loop, increasing amounts can read smaller states already updated for the current denomination, allowing reuse. Decreasing amounts instead read the previous-item layer at the smaller amount, limiting the current item to one use.

notes.title: Reusing Circular DP Slots Safely
notes.takeaway: A circular DP slot is a reusable box, not a permanent distance into the past; overwrite it only after its old answer's last consumer has read it.
notes.details: In a k-jump recurrence, the slot holding dp[i−k] is still needed for the jump of length k. Compute every candidate before replacing that slot with dp[i]; its index does not permanently identify a fixed distance into the past.

notes.title: Deriving Safe DP Update Order
notes.takeaway: Safety comes from which cells are read and overwritten, not a blanket backward-loop rule.
notes.details: Before compressing DP storage, identify which transitions require old values and which require updated values. Choose the loop direction from those dependencies; iterating backward is not a universal guarantee of safety.

notes.title: Mixing Rows in Unique Paths
notes.takeaway: One array may correctly contain two DP layers at once: old vertical and updated horizontal values are intentional when the recurrence asks for exactly that mixture.
notes.details: For a grid cell, the path count uses the cell above from the previous row and the cell to its left from the current row. A left-to-right one-array update intentionally preserves exactly this mixture.

notes.title: Freezing the Current BFS Level
notes.takeaway: If a loop must process the original batch, freeze its boundary before adding the next batch.
notes.details: Capture the queue size before processing a level, then process exactly that many nodes while appending their children. Rechecking a changing queue size can mix levels or end the current batch too early.

notes.title: Shared Cursors Determine Recursion Order
notes.takeaway: Independent recursive ranges can be processed in either order; one shared cursor forces the order in which its stream is consumed.
notes.details: A shared cursor reading postorder backward consumes root, right subtree, then left subtree. Reconstruction must follow that order; independent explicit ranges do not impose the same cursor dependency.

notes.title: Using Next Links as Worklists
notes.takeaway: A completed level’s next links can become the worklist for building the next level.
notes.details: Once a level is connected by next pointers, traverse those links to discover its children. Append each existing left child before its right child to build the next level's chain.

notes.title: Tracking Asymmetric BST Preorder Bounds
notes.takeaway: In BST preorder verification, upper bounds tighten on descent and relax on return, so they need a stack. The lower bound only tightens, so one variable suffices.
notes.details: For distinct-key BST preorder verification, popping ancestors models leaving completed subtrees and releases their upper bounds. The last popped value becomes the strongest lower bound, preventing later values from returning to a finished left region.

notes.title: Counting Unfinished Tree Serialization Slots
notes.takeaway: To validate a null-marked binary-tree preorder, you do not need to store every unfinished child position—only how many remain.
notes.details: Start with one pending root slot; a non-null token consumes one slot and creates two, while a null token only consumes one. Require a positive count before every token and zero after the final token; total counts alone cannot reject every invalid ordering.
