notes.title: Scanning Common Substrings by Diagonal
notes.takeaway: For longest common substring, each cell depends only on its preceding diagonal cell; scanning whole diagonals needs one streak instead of a row.
notes.details: Longest-common-substring states extend only the preceding diagonal match. Process one whole diagonal at a time, incrementing a streak on equality and resetting it on mismatch, while retaining the maximum streak across diagonals.

notes.title: Duplicate Paths Change Counting Results
notes.takeaway: Duplicate paths to the same choice do not change a minimum, but adding their counts overcounts the choice.
notes.details: In coin change, different orderings of the same combination may leave a minimum coin count unchanged. Adding those orderings as separate results overcounts when the required objects are combinations rather than sequences.

notes.title: Canonical Denomination Order for Combinations
notes.takeaway: Count combinations by fixing a denomination order: every multiplicity choice has one ordered representative, without sorting the input.
notes.details: Process coin denominations in one fixed index order so each combination has one representative grouped by denomination. Numeric sorting is unnecessary; consistency of the denomination order is what removes permutation duplicates.

notes.title: Counting a Subset and Its Complement
notes.takeaway: When choosing one side fixes its complement, count that choice once; multiplying counts would treat dependent choices as independent.
notes.details: When a partition is defined by assigning indices to S2, every remaining index is forced into S1. Count the valid S2 selections once; independently selecting both sides would allow reused or omitted elements.

notes.title: Largest Square Encodes Smaller Squares
notes.takeaway: At a fixed corner, a largest all-ones square of side k certifies every size 1 through k; one maximum replaces a whole Boolean size dimension.
notes.details: If the largest all-ones square ending at a bottom-right corner has side k, exactly one square of each side from 1 through k ends there. The single maximum therefore contributes k to the total count.

notes.title: Assigning Squares a Unique Corner
notes.takeaway: Count squares ending at a corner, not squares containing a cell: each square has one bottom-right owner, so summing contributions cannot duplicate it.
notes.details: Count all-ones squares by where they end, not by every cell they contain. Each square has exactly one bottom-right corner, so summing per-corner contributions counts it once.

notes.title: Counting Zeros After Reaching Target
notes.takeaway: Reaching the target is not always the end of a counting problem: unprocessed zeros still create distinct take-or-skip choices.
notes.details: A remaining zero can be included or skipped without changing the subset sum. Returning one immediately when the remaining target reaches zero can miss distinct index selections, so the counting base case must still account for unprocessed zeros.

notes.title: Tracking Optimal Length and Multiplicity
notes.takeaway: To count optimal solutions, keep quality and multiplicity: replace the count on improvement, and add counts on ties when the represented choices are disjoint.
notes.details: When extending increasing subsequences, a longer candidate replaces both the best length and its count; an equally long candidate adds its count. Addition is valid when the predecessor choices represent disjoint subsequences.

notes.title: Distinct Zero Choices Share a State
notes.takeaway: Taking a zero and skipping it can call the same child state, but they are different choices, so add that child's count twice.
notes.details: In the subset-counting formulation of Target Sum, including and excluding a zero reach the same remaining state. They still represent two distinct choices, so both transitions contribute the child's count.

notes.title: Interleaving Independent BST Insertion Orders
notes.takeaway: Independent subsequences can be interleaved without changing their internal order: choose positions, then multiply by each side’s valid reorderings.
notes.details: Keep the root first, choose the L positions occupied by left-subtree values among the next L+R positions, and multiply by each subtree's valid reorderings. This counts insertion orders, not preorder traversals; internal order within each chosen side-order is preserved.

notes.title: Unique Producers Remove Deduplication Needs
notes.takeaway: If every result has exactly one producer, a set adds no deduplication value.
notes.details: When deleting tree nodes, each surviving child of a deleted parent can be emitted exactly once by that parent. If the wrapper also handles the surviving original root once and output order is unrestricted, a set adds no deduplication benefit.

notes.title: Owning Leaf Pairs at Their LCA
notes.takeaway: Count each pair of leaves at its LCA: that is the unique node where they lie in opposite child subtrees.
notes.details: Two distinct leaves occur in opposite child subtrees only at their lowest common ancestor. Counting cross-child pairs there gives each pair one owner, avoiding duplicates at higher ancestors.

notes.title: Preserving Multiplicity in Distance Summaries
notes.takeaway: Compress equal distances into frequencies, not a set; equal distances can still represent different leaves.
notes.details: Multiple leaves at the same distance remain distinct pair candidates. Store their frequency rather than deduplicating the distance; qualifying left and right buckets contribute the product of their frequencies.

notes.title: Querying Prefixes Before Inserting Current
notes.takeaway: Query earlier prefixes before inserting the current one, or a zero target can count an empty path.
notes.details: For Path Sum III, query earlier ancestor-prefix frequencies before inserting the current prefix. Otherwise a zero target lets the current prefix pair with itself, incorrectly counting an empty path.

notes.title: Distinguishing BST Shapes from Insertion Orders
notes.takeaway: Count the resulting structures, not the different construction orders that happen to produce the same structure.
notes.details: For a fixed set of distinct keys, inorder ordering assigns values uniquely to each BST shape. Different insertion orders can produce that same shape, so they must not be counted separately when the requested objects are distinct BSTs.

notes.title: One Choice for an Empty Subtree
notes.takeaway: An empty subtree is one valid choice, not zero choices; otherwise pairing it with a nonempty subtree produces no combinations.
notes.details: When generating BSTs by pairing left and right subtree choices, an empty interval must return one empty-subtree choice. Returning no choices would make every pairing involving that empty side disappear.

notes.title: Fixed Row Order for N Queens
notes.takeaway: Fix one queen per row and a fixed row order: each recursion path represents one board, rather than another ordering of the same board.
notes.details: Place one queen per row and process rows in a fixed order while tracking occupied columns and diagonals. Each recursion path then identifies one board instead of another placement ordering of the same board.

notes.title: Isolating Exact GCD Pair Counts
notes.takeaway: 'Both values are divisible by d' counts GCDs that are multiples of d. Subtract the already-known larger multiples to isolate GCD exactly d.
notes.details: Choosing pairs among values divisible by d counts every pair whose GCD is a multiple of d. Process d downward and subtract the exact counts already computed for its larger multiples to obtain the count with GCD exactly d.

notes.title: Separating Complete and Extendable Tree Paths
notes.takeaway: Keep “best anywhere” separate from “the value my caller can extend.”
notes.details: A ZigZag helper must return a length compatible with the incoming edge direction, while a maximum-path-sum helper may return only one extendable downward arm. Keep the best completed path separate from either caller-facing result; a completed maximum-sum path may use both child arms.

notes.title: Choosing a Recursive Return Contract
notes.takeaway: Return what the caller needs: facts about the subtree, or the subtree that should replace it.
notes.details: A tree helper can return facts about its subtree or the root that should replace it. For a modifying helper, the caller must reconnect the returned pointer, which may be the existing node, a descendant, or null.

notes.title: Returning Height with Deepest Node Candidates
notes.takeaway: Return the candidate answer together with the information its parent needs to choose between candidates; a deepest-node LCA needs the subtree height too.
notes.details: Return both the candidate LCA of a subtree's deepest nodes and that subtree's height. Unequal child heights select the taller side's candidate; equal heights select the current node, while the returned height always describes the whole current subtree.

notes.title: Separating Path State from Shared Totals
notes.takeaway: Branch-local path state and shared aggregation have different jobs. Copy or restore the path state; deliberately share the total.
notes.details: A root-to-leaf number belongs to one branch and must be passed by value or restored before visiting a sibling. A shared total may intentionally aggregate both branches, provided it is reset for each top-level invocation.

notes.title: Leaving Out of Range Tokens Unread
notes.takeaway: A value that does not fit the current subtree can mean 'this subtree is finished,' not 'the whole input is invalid.' Leave it unread for an ancestor's next branch.
notes.details: A bounded BST-preorder parser consumes the next value only if it belongs to the current subtree. A non-fitting value may belong to an ancestor's later branch, so leave it unread and reject only if values remain after the complete parse.

notes.title: Checking Complete Input Consumption
notes.takeaway: Successfully parsing one complete structure is not the same as successfully parsing the whole input; check that nothing remains unread.
notes.details: A recursive serialization validator can successfully consume one tree while leaving extra tokens. The wrapper must require both successful subtree validation and an index at the end of the input; the helper must also reject missing tokens before reading them.
notes.code:
validateOneSubtree:
    if index >= token count: return false
    consume the next token (advance index even for #)
    if token is #: return true
    return validateLeftSubtree AND validateRightSubtree

validateWholeInput:
    index = 0
    valid = validateOneSubtree
    return valid AND index == token count

notes.title: Testing Leaves After Child Pruning
notes.takeaway: For repeated deletion of target-valued leaves, judge a node using the children that remain after recursion—not the children it originally had.
notes.details: Repeated target-leaf deletion can turn a former parent into a new removable leaf. Reconnect the recursively pruned children before deciding whether the current target-valued node is now a leaf.

notes.title: Passing Path Sums and Returning Survival
notes.takeaway: Send path information down; return whether any qualifying continuation survives up.
notes.details: For insufficient-path pruning, pass the accumulated ancestor sum down to evaluate original root-to-leaf paths. Return whether any qualifying continuation survives so the parent can decide which child links to keep.

notes.title: Preserving Original Leaf Semantics
notes.takeaway: A node becoming a leaf does not make it an original path endpoint.
notes.details: When qualification applies to original root-to-leaf paths, a node exposed by pruning does not become a new valid endpoint. Record or test its original leaf status before removing children.

notes.title: Evaluating Both Branches Before Combining
notes.takeaway: “Either branch succeeds” permits short-circuiting only if skipping the other branch also skips no required work.
notes.details: A pruning helper must visit both children even if either surviving branch is enough to keep the parent. Evaluate both recursive calls first, then combine their Boolean results; short-circuit OR can skip required mutations.

notes.title: Pruning Summaries After Counting Local Answers
notes.takeaway: Discard a summary when it cannot help an ancestor—not before counting the answers wholly inside its subtree.
notes.details: In bounded-distance leaf-pair counting, a leaf distance may be too large to help form a pair at any ancestor. Discard it from the returned summary only after counting valid pairs already formed inside the current subtree.

notes.title: Clamping Optional Child Path Gains
notes.takeaway: Clamping each optional child gain at zero turns four path-sum cases into one expression.
notes.details: In maximum path sum, a negative child branch can be omitted, so clamp each optional gain to zero. The through-node candidate then covers node-only, one-child, and two-child cases, while the caller receives only one extendable downward arm.

notes.title: Preserving Information Before Rewiring Links
notes.takeaway: Before overwriting a link, ask what information it is preserving; save only what the next step needs.
notes.details: Before replacing a tree pointer, determine whether its old target is still needed for the next connection. Save that attachment information separately instead of trying to recover it after the structure changes.

notes.title: Separating New Roots from Attachment Nodes
notes.takeaway: The root returned by a transformation is not necessarily the node where the caller must reconnect.
notes.details: In upside-down tree transformation, the transformed subtree's new root is different from the old left child used for local reconnection. Preserve both roles separately to avoid repeated right-chain searches that can make the transformation quadratic.

notes.title: Combining Downward Repair with Upward Recalculation
notes.takeaway: Fix only the next edge; recursion can propagate the requirement downward and restore exact values on the way back.
notes.details: For the increment-only children-sum transformation, repair the immediate deficit before recursing so the same local operation propagates downward. After the children are updated, set the parent to their final sum; these two phases fit in one recursive helper.

notes.title: Propagating Recursive Search Completion
notes.takeaway: Returning from the call that found the answer does not stop callers that were already waiting; guard the points where execution resumes.
notes.details: Finding the kth inorder value and returning from that frame does not stop its waiting ancestors. Propagate a success result or check a shared stop condition wherever execution resumes after a recursive call.

notes.title: Restoring Morris Threads After Failure
notes.takeaway: An answer may be known before an operation is safe to stop: temporary structural changes still have to be undone.
notes.details: Morris BST validation temporarily rewires predecessor links. After detecting an ordering violation, record failure but continue long enough to remove every temporary thread; returning immediately can leave the input tree corrupted.

notes.title: Separating Level Discovery from Contribution Scans
notes.takeaway: Stopping a contribution scan must not stop discovery of the next batch.
notes.details: For directional-prefix level sums, first gather children from every node in the current level. A later break in the summation loop must not prevent excluded nodes' children from appearing in subsequent levels.

notes.title: Finishing Component Traversal After Failure
notes.takeaway: Separate detecting a failure from finishing the traversal: if the outer loop relies on visited marks, an early return can split one component into several fake components.
notes.details: When an outer loop uses visited or color marks to identify components, detecting a coloring conflict must not leave the component half-visited. Set a failure flag and finish traversal so its unvisited tail is not counted later as a separate component.

notes.title: Guaranteeing Progress in Precomputed Jumps
notes.takeaway: A jump to a precomputed index still needs a progress argument: if that index can equal the current one, the loop can stall.
notes.details: A prefix-maximum index that includes the current position can point back to that same position. In a backward jump scan, continue from strictly before the chosen index so each iteration makes progress and the loop can terminate.

notes.title: Checking Bounds of Recursive Subproblems
notes.takeaway: Being inside the array is not enough: a recursive read must belong to the current subproblem.
notes.details: During traversal-based reconstruction, a potential child index may be inside the full array but outside the current subtree segment. Handle singleton subproblems and validate reads against the active segment, not only the container's bounds.

notes.title: Avoiding Revisits with Tree Arrival Edges
notes.takeaway: In a tree, remembering the node you arrived from is enough to avoid revisits; in a cyclic graph, it is not.
notes.details: When traversing a tree through child and parent links, skipping the node just visited prevents retracing the unique arrival edge. This relies on the absence of undirected cycles; general cyclic graphs need additional visited-state tracking.

notes.title: Representing an Iterator as Paused Traversal
notes.takeaway: An iterator is a traversal paused with just enough state to resume—not necessarily a precomputed list.
notes.details: A BST iterator can retain only the traversal state needed to resume inorder at the next request. It need not materialize the complete traversal before returning the first value.

notes.title: Accumulating Greater Values in Reverse Inorder
notes.takeaway: Choose an order that makes the aggregate incremental: reverse inorder turns BST suffix sums into one running sum.
notes.details: Reverse inorder visits BST values from greater to smaller. For the greater-sum transformation, a running total then contains the values already visited that contribute to the current node's replacement value.

notes.title: Capturing Right View with Right First DFS
notes.takeaway: Change visit order to make the answer the first item seen instead of the last.
notes.details: A right-first DFS encounters the right-view node first at each depth, so record only the first value for that depth. This changes which endpoint is easy to capture without changing the traversal's asymptotic complexity.

notes.title: Composing Vertical Traversal Ordering Rules
notes.takeaway: Let each mechanism supply one ordering: BFS supplies depth, enqueue order breaks ties, and the map orders columns.
notes.details: For vertical order with left-to-right ties, BFS provides increasing depth, left-before-right enqueueing provides tie order, and an ordered map provides column order. Those guarantees remove the need for a separate depth sort within each column.

notes.title: Understanding Stable Ordering Guarantees
notes.takeaway: Stability preserves an order you already established; it does not know the tie-breaking order you intended.
notes.details: A stable ordering operation preserves the existing input order among equivalent keys. It cannot create the intended left-to-right tie order unless the earlier traversal or collection step already established it.

notes.title: Scoping Prefix Frequencies to Ancestors
notes.takeaway: A DFS prefix map represents the current ancestor chain—not every prefix ever seen.
notes.details: In Path Sum III, the prefix-frequency map must describe only the active root-to-current ancestor chain. Insert before visiting descendants and decrement on return so a completed sibling branch cannot supply a false ancestor prefix.

notes.title: Making First Seen Mean Shallowest
notes.takeaway: 'First seen' means 'shallowest' only when the traversal order guarantees it. BFS supplies that guarantee; DFS needs an explicit depth comparison.
notes.details: For a tree's top view, BFS guarantees the first node encountered in each column has minimum depth. DFS can encounter a deeper node first and therefore needs an explicit per-column depth comparison.

notes.title: Deriving Postorder from Reversed Preorder
notes.takeaway: When node-last order feels awkward, reverse the desired order and look for an easy node-first traversal.
notes.details: Reverse the desired left-right-root order to obtain root-right-left, which is easy to generate as modified preorder. Reversing the collected result produces postorder; an explicit stack must push left before right to visit right first.

notes.title: Separating Zigzag Display from BFS Order
notes.takeaway: The queue decides visit order; the output decides display order. Zigzagging the answer does not require zigzagging the traversal.
notes.details: Keep queue traversal and child scheduling in ordinary left-to-right BFS order. Reverse only the completed level's output when needed, toggling direction once per level.

notes.title: Visiting Faulty Pointer Targets First
notes.takeaway: Changing traversal order can make the needed information available without storing it explicitly.
notes.details: When the one faulty right pointer targets a distinct node at the same depth strictly to its right, right-first DFS visits that target before the faulty owner. This ordering supplies the needed seen-node evidence without explicitly storing levels.

notes.title: Distinguishing Tree Edges from Added Links
notes.takeaway: A visited set prevents repeated traversal; it does not tell you which links belong to the structure you meant to measure.
notes.details: In a tree augmented with links between leaves, a visited set prevents repeated expansion but does not identify original child edges. Following added links can make graph distance differ from tree depth, so identify the intended structural edges before measuring height.

notes.title: Tracking Active Ancestors in Preorder
notes.takeaway: A preorder traversal cannot return to a subtree after finishing it.
notes.details: For preorder entries with required parents, pop finished subtrees until the stack top is the next entry's parent. If that parent is no longer active, the order is invalid: preorder cannot return to a completed subtree.

notes.title: Separating Match Starts from Consecutive Matching
notes.takeaway: Finding a start may search past nodes; matching from that start may not skip them.
notes.details: Finding where a linked-list pattern begins may search every tree node, but matching from a chosen start must follow consecutive downward nodes. Keep those jobs distinct so a failed match does not hide an overlapping valid start below it.

notes.title: Modeling DFS Entry Middle and Exit
notes.takeaway: Preorder, inorder, and postorder observe the same DFS lifecycle at entry, middle, and exit.
notes.details: Preorder records a node at entry, inorder after its left subtree, and postorder after both subtrees. An explicit node-and-state stack models the same recursive frame by remembering which checkpoint must resume next.

notes.title: Binary Searching a Preorder Partition
notes.takeaway: Binary search needs a monotone predicate, not sorted values.
notes.details: Within a valid distinct-key BST subtree's preorder segment, values greater than the root form a contiguous right-subtree suffix. That false-then-true predicate permits boundary search even though the segment is not sorted; arbitrary unsorted input does not provide this guarantee.

notes.title: Preserving First True Boundary Candidates
notes.takeaway: possible answer → keep mid; impossible answer → skip mid.
notes.details: In the first-true search variant that retains its answer inside the search bounds, a true midpoint remains a candidate, so set right to mid. A false midpoint and all earlier positions are impossible, so set left to mid+1.

notes.title: Using an Unreadable Boundary Sentinel
notes.takeaway: One-past-end can be a possible answer without being a readable element.
notes.details: A first-true boundary search may return one past the segment to mean no true position exists. With left less than right and a floor midpoint, reads remain inside the real segment; the final sentinel is an answer position, not an element to dereference.

notes.title: Separating Search Position from Best Candidate
notes.takeaway: The pointer exploring the search space and the best answer found so far are two different jobs.
notes.details: A floor or ceil search may need to traverse through a node that is not itself a valid answer. Keep the traversal pointer separate from the best valid candidate so exploring a promising subtree does not lose the saved answer or stall the search.

notes.title: Retaining an Extra Rank for Exclusion
notes.takeaway: To recompute the top k after excluding one contribution, retain the top k+1.
notes.details: To recover the top k contributions after excluding one child, retain the top k+1 beforehand. Preserve identity or multiplicity so exactly that child's contribution is removed, and use the problem's default when too few contributions exist.

notes.title: Locating Boundaries of Small Range Answers
notes.takeaway: A monotone answer with only K possible values is a staircase: find its change boundaries instead of recomputing every step.
notes.details:
If answers across an ordered sequence of updates are monotone and take only a small number of distinct values, many adjacent queries share one result. Search for change boundaries or use divide-and-conquer to identify constant intervals, accounting separately for the cost of each answer evaluation.

REVIEW NEEDED: Verify the exact source's claimed bound of at most 17 steps or boundaries against the allowed answer values, including −1. The general monotone-small-range takeaway does not depend on that numeric bound; evaluation-call counts and total runtime should also be distinguished.

notes.title: Ranking Perfect Subtrees by Height
notes.takeaway: If a quantity is a strictly increasing function of a cheaper representation, rank the representation and convert only the final answer.
notes.details: A perfect subtree with height h has size 2^h−1, so height and size induce the same ranking. Preserve duplicate heights when finding the kth subtree, then convert only the selected height if sizes are not already available.

notes.title: Evicting the Sorted Window Endpoint
notes.takeaway: The oldest value need not be the farthest; in a sorted closest-k window, it is still the only one an incoming larger value can evict.
notes.details: During increasing-order traversal for the closest k values, the queue front is the smallest retained value, not necessarily the farthest. An incoming larger value is compared against that left endpoint to decide whether the retained sorted window should advance.

notes.title: Binary Searching Complete Tree Occupancy
notes.takeaway: Completeness turns last-level occupancy into true…true, false…false; counting nodes becomes finding a boundary.
notes.details: A complete binary tree fills its last level from left to right without gaps. Existence by last-level position is therefore true followed by false, allowing a boundary search to determine how many positions are occupied.

notes.title: Relating Adjacent BST Keys by Ancestry
notes.takeaway: Adjacent BST keys must be ancestor-related: separate branches would force a key between them at their LCA.
notes.details: For distinct keys, immediate predecessor and successor among already-inserted values cannot lie in separate branches. Their lowest common ancestor would otherwise have a key strictly between them, contradicting their adjacency.

notes.title: Eliminating Impossible Two Sum Candidates
notes.takeaway: In a sorted two-sum scan, if the smallest candidate plus the largest remaining partner is still too small, no remaining partner can rescue that candidate.
notes.details: Compare the smallest remaining value from one BST with the largest remaining value from the other. If their sum is too small, discard the smaller candidate; if too large, discard the larger one, because no remaining partner can fix that candidate's sum.

notes.title: Checking Neighboring Occurrences on a Circle
notes.takeaway: For the nearest equal value on a circle, only the previous and next occurrences in circular index order can win.
notes.details: Store sorted occurrence indices for each value and locate the queried index in its list. Only its previous and next occurrences in circular order can be closest; apply wraparound distance, and return no match when the queried occurrence is the only one.

notes.title: Search The Sales Threshold
notes.takeaway: Binary-search a monotonic threshold, not necessarily the returned answer. Here, the number of balls above a height is monotonic even though profit is what we return.
notes.details: For diminishing inventory values, the number of balls strictly above a height decreases as that height rises. Search this boundary, then use arithmetic-series sums and a partial final level to compute profit without simulating every sale.

notes.title: Reject Impossible Digit Factors
notes.takeaway: Before searching for a zero-free digit product divisible by t, factor t: digits 1 through 9 cannot supply any prime outside 2, 3, 5 and 7.
notes.details: A product of nonzero decimal digits contains only the prime factors 2, 3, 5, and 7. Divide these factors out of the required divisor before searching; any remaining prime makes divisibility impossible.

notes.title: Positive Sums Support Sliding Windows
notes.takeaway: With positive values, a window can shrink from the left until its sum is valid; neither pointer ever needs to move backward.
notes.details: For the longest contiguous segment of positive values with sum at most a budget, extending right can only increase the sum and removing left can only decrease it. Each pointer moves forward at most once per element, giving linear total work.

notes.title: Check Validity After Shrinking
notes.takeaway: Shrinking a valid segment is not automatically safe: removing its left edge may reset the process and change every later decision.
notes.details: In Good Schedule, removing the first position restarts the process with need equal to 1. That reset can change later decisions and create a violation, so a valid segment does not imply its left-trimmed suffix is valid.

notes.title: Summarize Reachability By Its Boundary
notes.takeaway: When every shorter forward jump is allowed, indices reachable from the start form a prefix; its farthest boundary summarizes the entire reachable set.
notes.details: In Jump Game, an allowed forward jump also permits every shorter jump. Reachable intervals therefore overlap into a prefix, allowing one farthest-reachable index to summarize the set instead of storing every reachable position.

notes.title: Exclude The Uncuttable Root
notes.takeaway: Exclude the root because there is no edge above it—not because zero totals need a special case.
notes.details: An equal partition requires cutting an existing parent edge, so the whole tree is never a candidate detachable subtree. Search only non-root nodes, including when the total is zero, and reject null children before testing their sums.

notes.title: Cover Circular Endpoint Exclusions
notes.takeaway: If two endpoints cannot both be chosen, solve the two cases excluding one endpoint; neither case has to force the other endpoint in.
notes.details: A valid circular-house selection skips the first house, the last house, or both. Taking the better linear solution after excluding each endpoint covers all valid selections without requiring the opposite endpoint to be selected.

notes.title: Extend Transitive Divisibility Chains
notes.takeaway: When compatibility is transitive, checking a chain's last element can certify compatibility with the whole chain.
notes.details: In a valid divisibility chain, every earlier selected value divides the final value. If that final value divides a new candidate, transitivity certifies compatibility with the whole chain using one divisibility check.

notes.title: Justify Discarding DP Alternatives
notes.takeaway: DP preserves relevant alternatives; greedy needs a reason those alternatives can be discarded without losing an optimum.
notes.details: A DP state retains alternatives that can affect future profit, such as holding or being constrained by a cooldown. Replacing these alternatives with a greedy choice requires a reason that the discarded histories cannot lead to a better result.

notes.title: Interpret Adjusted Purchase Thresholds
notes.takeaway: A greedy variable can be an adjusted break-even threshold, not a literal purchase price: provisional profit can still be extended into a later sale.
notes.details: In the stock-with-fee greedy method, buyCost can become an adjusted break-even threshold after recording provisional profit. It need not identify an actual purchase, and recording today's gain does not prevent extending the same opportunity to a later sale.

notes.title: Compare Drops Against Extra Fees
notes.takeaway: With unlimited trades, a transaction fee, and no cooldown, splitting a trade beats holding only when the peak-to-valley drop exceeds the extra fee.
notes.details: With unlimited trades and no cooldown, selling at a peak and rebuying at a later valley changes profit relative to holding by peak minus valley minus one extra fee. A larger drop favors splitting, equality ties, and the drop may span multiple days.

notes.title: Largest Divisible Subset: LIS-style DP works, tails doesn’t
notes.takeaway:
- Sort first. Extend an earlier chain when nums[i] % nums[j] == 0.
- Don’t keep only the smallest ending value for each length: 9 can follow 3, but cannot follow 2.
notes.details:
dp[i] = longest divisible chain ending at nums[i].

Checking the last element is enough: if 2 divides 4, and 4 divides 8, then 2 also divides 8.

But LIS’s tails shortcut loses useful options here. For [2,3,9], keeping only [2] as the length-one chain discards [3]—so we miss [3,9].

In LIS, a smaller endpoint is at least as easy to extend. In divisibility, it isn’t.

notes.title: Join Subsequences At One Peak
notes.takeaway: Combine two optimal halves at the same boundary; independent global maxima may not belong to a compatible whole.
notes.details: For a bitonic subsequence, combine the increasing subsequence ending at an index with the decreasing subsequence starting at that same index, subtracting the shared peak once. Independent global maxima can occur at incompatible positions and cannot safely be added.

notes.title: Commit Earlier Wildcard Block Matches
notes.takeaway: In wildcard matching, an earlier feasible intermediate block leaves at least as much suffix; the next star can absorb the gap, so choices before it need not be revisited.
notes.details: For an intermediate fixed block followed by another star, an earlier feasible match leaves at least as much source text for the remainder. The following star can absorb the extra gap, so moving that block later cannot unlock a suffix that the earlier placement excludes.

notes.title: Merge Candy Bounds By Maximum
notes.takeaway: When left and right neighbors impose separate lower bounds, take their maximum to satisfy both—not their sum.
notes.details: The two directional passes impose lower bounds from the original left and right neighbors. Retain the maximum of those bounds to satisfy both with the fewest candies; summing overpays, while sorting would destroy the adjacency constraints.

notes.title: Order Tasks By Energy Buffer
notes.takeaway: For minimum initial energy, sort by minimum minus actual, descending: the buffer left after paying a task's cost matters, not its minimum alone.
notes.details:
For each task, minimum minus actual measures the required buffer beyond its consumed energy. Process larger buffers first, then simulate the order by adding only the deficit needed before each task and subtracting its actual cost.

REVIEW NEEDED: The source's surrounding prose reverses the ordering direction even though the takeaway, example, and algorithm specify descending minimum minus actual. Review that source wording before publication.

notes.title: Bound A Restricted Minimum Globally
notes.takeaway: A global surrogate minimum can cover a restricted region when true cost never exceeds the surrogate and equals it inside that region. Evaluate the candidate's true cost.
notes.details: In Minimum Influence, true cost never exceeds p+c and equals p+c within the center region. The globally smallest p+c item, evaluated using its true cost, is therefore no worse than any center-region candidate even if the selected item lies outside that region.

notes.title: Compare Equivalent Reading Bundles
notes.takeaway: Compare options that satisfy the same requirement: one book liked by both versus one Alice-only book plus one Bob-only book.
notes.details: One both-liked book and a pair containing one Alice-only plus one Bob-only book each satisfy one additional requirement for both readers. Sort the three categories and compare these equivalent bundles, checking that each candidate bundle is available before choosing.

notes.title: Prioritize The Dominant Row Bit
notes.takeaway: Making the highest bit 1 is safe when that bit is worth more than every possible loss in all lower bits combined.
notes.details: In a binary row, the highest bit is worth one more than every lower bit combined, so making it 1 outweighs any lower-bit loss caused by that row flip. Once all first bits are 1, choose each remaining column's orientation independently to maximize its number of 1s.

notes.title: Exchange For Earliest Legal Placement
notes.takeaway: To prove the earliest legal placement is safe, exchange it with a later optimal placement: left-side legality remains, and the space available to the right only increases.
notes.details: In Social Distance, place a new 1 only when it is far enough from the latest left 1 and the nearest original right 1. Replacing a later optimal placement with this earlier legal position preserves left-side legality and only enlarges the gaps to placements on the right.

notes.title: Close Valid Teams Immediately
notes.takeaway: After sorting team-size requirements, close a team as soon as it is valid; giving it extra people cannot increase the number of teams.
notes.details: After sorting requirements, the current largest requirement determines when the growing team is valid. Closing it immediately preserves unused people for later teams; adding extra members to an already valid team cannot increase the team count.

notes.title: Claim A Component At Its Entrance
notes.takeaway: To maximize a region you can secure, start at its entrance: any deeper choice gets at most the same component.
notes.details: Removing the first player's node conceptually leaves its left, right, and parent-side components. Starting at a component's adjacent entrance secures the entire component, while a deeper start cannot secure more; a winning response exists exactly when one component contains a majority of nodes.

notes.title: Stop After One Compatible Subtree
notes.takeaway: Once a split fixes independent left and right subproblems, one successful left answer is enough; enumerating its alternatives cannot repair the right side.
notes.details: With repeated traversal labels, each candidate root occurrence fixes both subtree sizes and traversal ranges. For that fixed split, any successful left reconstruction suffices when seeking one tree: a different left shape cannot change whether the independently fixed right range is reconstructible.

notes.title: Raise The Smaller Branch Root
notes.takeaway: Increasing a shared parent cannot close a difference between its branches; increase the smaller branch’s root to lift every path in it together.
notes.details: After balancing each child subtree internally, increasing their shared parent changes both path totals equally and cannot close the gap. Increasing the smaller child's root by that gap raises every path on that side together, achieving the required adjustment without separate payments at each leaf.

notes.title: Prove Coin Moves Per Edge
notes.takeaway: One exit edge forces a subtree’s net transfer: summing unavoidable crossings gives the optimum when those flows are achievable.
notes.details: A subtree has only one edge connecting it to the outside, so its coin surplus or deficit forces that many net crossings of the parent edge. Summing these edge-wise lower bounds proves optimality when the distribution process realizes all of them.

notes.title: Preorder Values Force Child Order
notes.takeaway: If no later decision can change the next required item, the current choice is forced—not a branch to optimize.
notes.details: When two child roots have distinct values, the next required preorder value determines which child must be visited first. If it names the right child, flipping the current node is unavoidable; later choices cannot alter that next visit.

notes.title: Separate Termination From Minimum Swaps
notes.takeaway: Permanent progress proves termination; a matching lower bound proves minimality.
notes.details: A level-sorting swap procedure can make permanent progress and still need a separate argument that its swap count is minimal. The permutation's cycle-count lower bound supplies that optimality argument, rather than progress alone.

notes.title: Consume BST Values As Streams
notes.takeaway: Sorted-order algorithms can operate on streams: BST iterators let you merge or scan opposite ends without materializing both traversals.
notes.details: Inorder iterators expose BST values in sorted order without storing complete traversals. Two iterators can feed a sorted merge lazily; account separately for their temporary traversal state and the space required by the returned answer.

notes.title: Distinguish Construction From Unique Recovery
notes.takeaway: Constructing one compatible answer and recovering the unique original answer are different requirements.
notes.details: Repeated labels in preorder and inorder can permit zero, one, or several compatible trees. Returning the first successful reconstruction proves existence only; it neither recovers a uniquely determined original nor enumerates every valid tree.

notes.title: Decode Paths From Shifted Labels
notes.takeaway: Adding one to a zero-based binary-tree label exposes its path: skip the leading one, then zero means left and one means right.
notes.details: For labels with children 2x+1 and 2x+2, shifting to x+1 makes left and right children append binary 0 and 1. Skip the leading root bit of target+1 and follow the remaining bits, rejecting the target if any required child is missing.

notes.title: Normalize Width Indices Without Compression
notes.takeaway: Preserve distances and shift the origin; normalization removes irrelevant offsets, not meaningful gaps.
notes.details: Subtracting the same first index from every position on a level preserves all differences and therefore the width. Renumbering only the present nodes consecutively would erase meaningful gaps; normalization shifts the origin but does not compress the level.

notes.title: Rebuild For Balance Not Original Shape
notes.takeaway: “Balance this BST” does not mean preserve its shape: if only values and balance matter, rebuilding is allowed.
notes.details: Balancing a BST requires preserving its values and search ordering, not its old shape. An inorder sequence can therefore be rebuilt around middle elements even though that sequence does not uniquely identify the original tree.

notes.title: Compare Addition Trees By Multiplicity
notes.takeaway: For addition-only expressions, equivalence is equal variable multiplicities—not equal tree shapes.
notes.details: When addition is the only operator, rearranging leaves or parentheses does not change the expression. Compare the number of occurrences of each variable, including repetitions, rather than requiring equal tree shapes or traversal order.

notes.title: Distinguish Insertion Order From Preorder
notes.takeaway: Insertion order is not preorder: left- and right-subtree insertions can interleave, so a contiguous split may not exist.
notes.details: A BST insertion sequence identifies the root with its first value, but subsequent left- and right-subtree insertions can interleave. Do not assume that all left-subtree values form a contiguous block as they would in a preorder traversal.

notes.title: Store A Continuation Before Flattening
notes.takeaway: A splice point need not be the final tail; it can hold a continuation that later rewrites move behind unfinished work.
notes.details: While flattening a binary tree, a splice endpoint can temporarily hold the original right-side continuation before the left subtree is fully flattened. Later pointer rewrites move that continuation behind the remaining work, so the endpoint need not already be the final tail.

notes.title: Allow Prefix Trees To Be Reparented
notes.takeaway: Build a correct structure for the prefix you have; a parent link need not be permanent to be useful now.
notes.details: During maximum-binary-tree construction, maintain a valid tree for the prefix processed so far. A later value may change an earlier parent link; requiring every initial link to be permanent prevents useful incremental construction.

notes.title: Translate Zigzag Labels Before Navigation
notes.takeaway: Convert to ordinary coordinates, do the easy operation there, then convert back.
notes.details: Zigzag numbering obscures the ordinary parent relationship. Translate a label into the corresponding ordinary tree coordinate, perform the parent operation there, and translate back into the required zigzag numbering.

notes.title: Separate List Head From Append Tail
notes.takeaway: Dummy remembers the beginning; tail keeps appending.
notes.details: When linking the next tree level, a dummy node preserves its beginning while a tail pointer advances as children are appended. These roles must remain separate so moving the append position does not lose the level's start.

notes.title: Serialize Missing Child Positions Too
notes.takeaway: To serialize a general binary tree, preserve the missing positions as well as the values. One traversal with null markers can encode what a values-only traversal loses.
notes.details: A values-only traversal can confuse a left-only child with a right-only child. A defined traversal format with explicit null markers preserves those missing positions and supports reconstruction even when node values repeat.

notes.title: Separate DSU Links From Tree Parents
notes.takeaway: A DSU parent links a node toward a component representative; it is not the node's parent in the input tree.
notes.details: DSU links lead to component representatives and may change during path compression or union; they do not encode the proposed tree's actual edges. Track incoming tree edges separately, and compare find results rather than raw DSU parent entries when checking component membership.

notes.title: Keep Filtered Digit Indices Separate
notes.takeaway: A filtered array creates a second index space. A position in the original string is not a position among its nonzero digits.
notes.details: The concatenation prefix structure is indexed among nonzero digits, while the digit-sum prefix structure uses original string positions. Convert a query's endpoints into the filtered index space before extracting the concatenation, and return zero when that filtered range is empty.

notes.title: Read Comparators As Ordering Questions
notes.takeaway: comp(a, b) answers one question: 'Should a come before b?'
notes.details: Read comp(a,b) as whether a should precede b. Ascending numeric order uses a<b and descending order uses a>b; a false result alone does not distinguish equivalence from b preceding a.

notes.title: Query Virtual Row Flips
notes.takeaway: You do not have to perform a transformation to query its result: after normalizing each row's first bit to 1, a cell is 1 exactly when its original bit equals that row's first bit.
notes.details: To normalize a row's first bit to 1, flip the row only if that original bit is 0. After this virtual operation, a cell is 1 exactly when its original value matches the row's original first bit, so column counts need not mutate the matrix.

notes.title: Model Scrambled Digits As Counts
notes.takeaway: Scrambling destroys order; only the digit counts survive. Work with the multiset, not the original positions.
notes.details: Once the digits have been scrambled, their original positions carry no information about the intended chain. Model the available digit multiset, then seek blocks whose values satisfy the successive digit-sum relationships.

notes.title: Validate Tokens Before Numeric Conversion
notes.takeaway: Validate the characters before converting the token to a number; successful numeric conversion is not proof that the entire token was valid.
notes.details: For an IP component, first enforce the allowed characters, length, and applicable leading-zero rules before converting its value. Numeric conversion can accept a valid prefix of a malformed token, so successful conversion does not establish full-token validity.

notes.title: Attach Predecessors To DP States
notes.takeaway: A predecessor belongs to a DP state, not to the traversal globally; one 'last chosen' variable cannot represent many alternative optimal histories.
notes.details: Each LCS table cell represents its own optimal subproblem and needs its own chosen predecessor state for reconstruction. A single global last-match variable mixes alternative histories and cannot represent all paths through the table.

notes.title: LIS Tails Are Not A Witness
notes.takeaway: A table of best representatives need not describe one realizable solution: each LIS tails slot may summarize a different underlying subsequence.
notes.details: Each LIS tails slot represents the best ending value for one subsequence length, potentially from a different subsequence. For input [2,3,4,1], the final tails [1,3,4] is not a subsequence of the input, so the table alone cannot be returned as the reconstructed LIS.

notes.title: Length Equality Does Not Transfer Witnesses
notes.takeaway: Equal optimal lengths do not make reconstructed witnesses interchangeable: LCS(s, reverse(s)) gives the LPS length, but an arbitrary reconstructed LCS need not be palindromic.
notes.details: The LCS length of a string and its reverse equals the longest-palindromic-subsequence length. This equality does not make every reconstructed LCS palindromic, so producing a palindrome requires reconstruction logic that preserves the needed structure.

notes.title: Freeze Concrete LIS Predecessor Indices
notes.takeaway: Store a predecessor's concrete original index, not a live reference to a mutable best-representative slot; later improvements then cannot rewrite an earlier solution path.
notes.details: An LIS predecessor link should store the selected element's original index at the time the link is created. Later replacing a best-tail slot then improves future choices without changing the already recorded chain of earlier elements.

notes.title: Clone Shared Templates At Return
notes.takeaway: Build shared templates once; pay for independent copies only at the return boundary.
notes.details: Memoized full-binary-tree construction can reuse subtree templates while assembling candidates. If returned trees must be independent, clone each final answer at the boundary instead of repeatedly cloning intermediate templates during construction.

notes.title: Choose Whether Cloning Preserves Sharing
notes.takeaway: Memoizing a clone by source address preserves sharing; copying each occurrence independently removes it.
notes.details: Caching clones by source address creates one copy per original node and therefore preserves aliasing. To turn shared full-binary-tree templates into independent trees, allocate a fresh node for every occurrence, including repeated occurrences within a single result.

notes.title: Register Clones Before Following Cycles
notes.takeaway: When cloning cyclic references, publish the copy before following its links; a cycle must find an existing identity.
notes.details: When random pointers can form cycles, create and cache a node's clone before recursively cloning its outgoing references. A self-reference or cycle then finds the existing copy; delaying registration until recursion returns can recurse indefinitely.

notes.title: Distinguish Persistence From Independent Copies
notes.takeaway: Leaving the original unchanged is not the same as producing an independent copy.
notes.details: Path copying can leave the original BST unchanged while the split outputs still share untouched subtrees with it. If outputs must be fully independent of the original, deep-copy the whole input before splitting, paying linear time and new-node storage.

notes.title: Memoization Cannot Shrink Required Output
notes.takeaway: Memoization removes repeated construction, not the cost of an exponentially large answer.
notes.details: Caching the list of full binary trees for each subtree size avoids rebuilding that list in repeated calls. It does not remove the need to produce the full set of requested results, whose size remains exponential.

notes.title: Index Ranges Still Permit Repeated Scans
notes.takeaway: Passing indices removes copying, not rescanning; a smaller representation does not automatically make the algorithm linear.
notes.details: Passing substring boundaries avoids allocating child-string copies during tree parsing. If each recursive call still scans its range to find matching brackets, repeated scanning remains and the representation change alone does not establish linear time.

notes.title: Append Into One Output Buffer
notes.takeaway: Build the final output once instead of rebuilding every descendant’s output at each ancestor.
notes.details: Returning a completed child string and embedding it into each ancestor's string repeatedly copies descendant output. A traversal that appends node tokens and parentheses directly into one shared answer avoids rebuilding those already written portions.

notes.title: Count Iterator Movement As Work
notes.takeaway: Logarithmic comparisons do not imply logarithmic work if reaching the midpoint takes linear iterator steps.
notes.details: Generic std::lower_bound performs logarithmically many comparisons, but map iterators cannot jump directly to a midpoint. Linear iterator movement can dominate the operation, so comparison count alone does not establish logarithmic running time.

notes.title: Charge Moves To Size Doublings
notes.takeaway: If every expensive move at least doubles the containing size, an element can make only logarithmically many moves.
notes.details: In the light-edge analysis of DSU on tree, moving upward across a light edge at least doubles the containing subtree size. Since that size starts at least at 1 and cannot exceed n, any fixed element can incur only logarithmically many such expensive crossings.

notes.title: Include Empty Output Cells In Complexity
notes.takeaway: A sparse input can require a dense output; empty cells still impose real time and space costs.
notes.details: Printing a binary tree as a dense grid requires materializing its empty cells as well as its node labels. If the required grid has C cells, both time and output storage have an unavoidable lower bound of Ω(C), even for a sparse input tree.

notes.title: Cheap Ranges Still Need Equality Work
notes.takeaway: Indices make ranges cheap to store, not automatically cheap to compare.
notes.details: A preorder serialization with null markers lets each subtree be stored as a range into one shared sequence. This saves copied storage, but directly comparing two ranges of length m still costs O(m); indices alone do not create constant-time equality checks.

notes.title: Count Subtree Visits Per Node
notes.takeaway: For repeated subtree traversals, count how often each node can be visited instead of multiplying two loose worst cases.
notes.details: After reducing repeated flip queries by parity, each complete-tree label starts at most one traversal. A node is visited only by traversals rooted at itself or its ancestors, so its O(log(n+1)) ancestor count gives a sharper total bound than multiplying two independent worst cases; this argument would not give the same bound for a chain.

notes.title: Amortize Across A Guaranteed Sequence
notes.takeaway: Amortized cost bounds the total over a sequence. It does not promise that each operation is cheap, and it is not an average over random inputs.
notes.details: Amortized analysis bounds total work across a sequence and divides that bound among the operations. Individual operations may still be expensive, but they must be infrequent enough to keep the sequence bound; this is not an expectation over random inputs.
notes.code:
Total cost = O(n) + (n - 1) × O(1) = O(n)
Amortized cost = total / n = O(1)

notes.title: Consume One Exponent Bit Per Step
notes.takeaway: Binary exponentiation is logarithmic because every iteration consumes one bit of the exponent—not merely because some iterations double a value.
notes.details: Binary exponentiation halves the remaining exponent each iteration, using its low bit to decide whether to multiply the result. Doubling a progress counter and then finishing with single increments does not provide this guarantee and can leave a linear remainder phase.

notes.title: Test Small Cases Before Guessing Formulas
notes.takeaway: When the formula is unclear, brute-force small cases to get ground truth before guessing the formula.
notes.details: When a contribution formula is unclear, enumerate small valid configurations and compare their exact results with candidate formulas. These cases expose incorrect guesses and suggest patterns, but a pattern observed in small cases still needs justification before generalizing.

notes.title: Constant Answers Can Hide Broken States
notes.takeaway: If every valid input has the same yes/no answer, passing tests can hide a completely broken recurrence.
notes.details: Under Stone Game's guarantees, every valid input has the same true result. Passing the final yes/no tests therefore cannot establish that a DP implementation computed its internal score-difference states correctly.

notes.title: Compare Exact Values Before Reducing
notes.takeaway: Modulo preserves congruence, not ordering. Compare exact values; apply modulo only after the decision.
notes.details: Modulo reduction preserves congruence but can reverse the relative order of two values. In Maximum XOR Product, construct and compare the exact factors within their supported numeric range, then reduce them for the final modular multiplication.

notes.title: Cap Values At Their Saturation Threshold
notes.takeaway: If every value beyond a threshold has the same effect on all future operations, store the threshold sentinel instead of the exact huge value.
notes.details:
When an LCM is used only in floor(m/lcm), every value above m produces the same zero contribution, so a sentinel m+1 is sufficient. For positive inputs and a representable m+1, divide by the gcd first and compare against cap/b before multiplying to avoid overflow.

REVIEW NEEDED: The preserved C++ comment claims (a/g)*b < (a*b)/g, but the expressions are mathematically equal; dividing first reduces the intermediate product, not the exact result. The cap implementation also assumes positive inputs and a representable m+1.

notes.title: Bound Intermediate Width Arithmetic Separately
notes.takeaway: A bounded final answer does not imply bounded intermediate arithmetic.
notes.details: A narrow deep tree can have enormous absolute complete-tree indices even when its reported width is small. Normalize indices and check the arithmetic used to derive children; a bounded final result does not make every algebraically equivalent machine expression safe.

notes.title: Separate Coin Direction From Move Count
notes.takeaway: For a subtree connected to the rest of a tree by one edge, its signed coin balance says what must cross that edge; the magnitude says how many moves it costs.
notes.details: For a subtree, coins minus nodes is its signed balance. A positive balance must leave through its parent edge and a negative balance must enter; the absolute value is the number of one-edge transfers contributed by that connection.

notes.title: Count Coin Journeys Edge By Edge
notes.takeaway: Count a journey one edge at a time; you may not need to identify its start and destination.
notes.details: A coin moving across three tree edges contributes three moves, one on each edge. Summing the required transfers across edges accounts for complete journeys without assigning individual coins to destinations or returning explicit travel distances.

notes.title: Propagate Forced Game Outcomes Backward
notes.takeaway: A game state is winning if one move wins, but losing only when every legal move loses; propagate those proofs backward from terminal states.
notes.details: In Cat and Mouse, one child outcome that wins for the current mover proves a parent win. A parent loss requires proving every legal move wins for the opponent, tracked by exhausting its remaining degree; states left unresolved after this backward propagation are draws.

notes.title: Use The Current Player's Score Advantage
notes.takeaway: Measure a game's score advantage for the player to move; subtracting the child's advantage handles both the turn switch and optimal opposition without a player flag.
notes.details: Define a Stone Game subproblem as the best score advantage available to the player whose turn it is. After taking a pile, subtract the child's advantage because the child describes the opponent's best response, making a separate player identity flag unnecessary.

notes.title: Parity Strategies Give A Lower Bound
notes.takeaway: In the even-pile Stone Game, equal parity sums guarantee a tie strategy—not that optimal play must tie.
notes.details:
In an even-pile variant allowing equal even-index and odd-index totals, committing to either parity guarantees at least a tie. That guarantee does not rule out a better strategy that wins, so parity equality alone does not determine the optimal result.

REVIEW NEEDED: Equal parity sums imply an even total, so this case lies outside the standard Stone Game odd-total guarantee. Present it as variant analysis rather than as a valid input under that guarantee.

notes.title: Tree Moves Can Block Whole Regions
notes.takeaway: A move can claim one node and cut off many more; alternating turns do not imply alternating shares of the remaining territory.
notes.details: In the binary-tree coloring game, claiming a junction can cut the opponent off from many still-uncolored nodes. Because a blocked player must pass, alternating turns do not imply that the initially shared territory will be divided into alternating or nearly equal shares.

notes.title: Start or Extend a Contiguous Subarray
notes.takeaway: For a contiguous subarray, choose whether to start here or extend the current segment—not skip an interior element.
notes.details: For a maximum-sum non-empty subarray ending at i, bestEnd[i] = max(a[i], bestEnd[i-1] + a[i]). A restart discards the entire previous segment; it does not keep an earlier piece while skipping an interior element. In the fixed-k signed-array discussion, apply this after assigning each value its positive or negative contribution. This does not by itself solve how to choose k.

notes.title: Remember Subarray Boundaries Without Parents
notes.takeaway: A subarray is identified by its start and end; reconstructing a subsequence may require remembering which indices were chosen.
notes.details: For start-or-extend DP, keep currentStart. When restarting at index i, set currentStart = i. Whenever the global best improves, save currentStart and i as the answer boundaries. No parent array is needed because all indices between the two boundaries belong to the segment. For non-empty subarrays, initialize from a real element so an all-negative input is handled correctly. Choose a consistent tie policy if several segments are optimal.

notes.title: Avoid Duplicates: Unique Construction Paths
notes.takeaway:
• Sorted vowel strings: Choose first vowel v; remaining characters can use only v or later vowels. Each string has one first-character branch.
• Parentheses: Build (inside)outside. First opening bracket’s matching close uniquely fixes the split.
• Unique-digit numbers: Start with 1–9; append unused digits only at the end (0 allowed afterward). Each result has one previous prefix. Arbitrary-position insertion can count it twice.
• Equal-minimum contributions: Previous strictly smaller + next smaller-or-equal assigns each interval to its rightmost minimum. Reverse the strictness for the leftmost. One owner → counted once.
• No duplicates: Smaller results must be unique; generate each choice or combination once.
notes.details:
The common idea: choose a decomposition that each finished answer determines uniquely. This lets us generate answers without a deduplication set, provided recursive results are unique and every choice or combination is generated once.

SORTED VOWEL STRINGS
Number a, e, i, o, u as 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. At f(remaining, minVowel), choose the first vowel c from minVowel through 4, then build the rest with f(remaining - 1, c). Keeping c allowed permits repeated vowels; requiring c+1 would incorrectly forbid repeats. Start with f(n, 0). Each finished string has exactly one first character, and its remaining suffix belongs to exactly one recursive result. Different first-character branches cannot produce the same string. This is a choice made at every recursive step, not a requirement that all strings start with the same vowel.

If generating strings, the zero-length result is one empty string, f(0, minVowel) = [""], not an empty list. If only counting, remaining == 0 returns 1 and the state returns the sum of its branches; no current string or vector of answers is needed. Count Sorted Vowel Strings asks for the count, while Generate Parentheses asks for the actual strings.

PARENTHESES
Here n counts pairs. Inside and outside must each be valid parentheses strings. For every x from 0 to n - 1, choose x pairs inside and n - x - 1 pairs outside. Combine every inside/outside pair as "(" + inside + ")" + outside. The base list is f(0) = [""].

Scan a finished parentheses string from its first opening bracket. The first point where opening and closing counts balance identifies that opening bracket's matching close, not necessarily the first closing bracket in the string. That position uniquely fixes inside, outside, and x. Different splits therefore cannot produce the same finished string.

UNIQUE-DIGIT NUMBERS
Start a positive number with one of 1–9, then append each unused digit only at the right end. Zero is allowed after the first digit if unused. Every finished number has exactly one previous prefix: remove its last digit. Provided each prefix and append choice is generated once, two branches cannot generate the same number.

Inserting a digit at every possible position loses that uniqueness. For example, start with 1 and insert 2 at the end to get 12; or start with 2 and insert 1 at the beginning to get the same 12. Multiplying by the number of insertion positions therefore overcounts. Appending only at the end gives one insertion position, not len positions.

Unused-digit tracking prevents repeated digits WITHIN one number. The unique-prefix construction prevents generating the SAME number multiple times. These are different requirements. Leading zeros must remain forbidden: otherwise different digit strings such as 1 and 01 could represent the same integer. Count the number zero separately.

For length-only counting, every valid positive prefix of length len−1 has used exactly len−1 digits, regardless of whether zero is among them. There are 10−(len−1) unused choices to append, so separate zero/nonzero states are unnecessary: dp[1]=9 and dp[len]=dp[len−1]×(11−len) for 2≤len≤10. In LC357, n≤8; the answer for 0≤x<10^n is 1+dp[1]+...+dp[n], with the initial 1 counting zero. For n=0, return 1.

EQUAL-MINIMUM CONTRIBUTIONS
For subarray-minimum contribution counting, an interval with several equal minima needs exactly one owner. Use L[i] = previous strictly smaller and R[i] = next smaller-or-equal. The interval is assigned to its rightmost minimum: an earlier equal minimum is blocked by the equal value to its right. Reversing the strictness (previous smaller-or-equal, next strictly smaller) assigns it to its leftmost minimum.

For heights [2,2], with rightmost ownership, index 0 owns [0]; index 1 owns [1] and [0,1]. Each interval is counted once. For all-one submatrix counting with the bottom row fixed, multiply the number of owned column intervals by height[i], giving 2 + 4 = 6 rectangles here.

Both-strict boundaries count an interval once per equal minimum occurrence. Both-nonstrict boundaries miss intervals containing multiple equal minima. Equality does not invalidate the rectangle or subarray; it decides which equal minimum counts it. This is an ownership convention for contribution counting, not a universal rule for every monotonic-stack problem.

WATCH OUT
Vectors do not cause duplicates; ambiguous construction paths do. Allowing every arbitrary split can produce "aaa" both as "a" + "aa" and as "aa" + "a". A unique outer decomposition is not enough if smaller result lists already contain duplicates or the same choice or combination is generated repeatedly. Appending is not a universal deduplication trick; the proof depends on unique parents, unique choices and an unambiguous representation.
