- https://leetcode.com/problems/count-numbers-with-unique-digits/description/
- https://leetcode.com/problems/count-submatrices-with-all-ones/description/

notes.title: Choosing the Right Catalan Index
notes.takeaway: Match the problem's size to the Catalan index: m matrices → C_(m-1), v polygon vertices → C_(v-2), and N total nodes in an ordered full binary tree → C_((N-1)/2) when N is odd.
notes.details:
A Catalan formula is useful only after identifying what its index counts.

• m matrices or operands, m ≥ 1: C_(m-1) full binary parenthesizations, preserving their order. This counts the possible groupings; it does not find the minimum matrix-multiplication cost.
• A convex polygon with v ≥ 3 fixed vertices: C_(v-2) triangulations using noncrossing diagonals. The vertices are distinguished; do not identify answers under rotation or reflection.
• An ordered full binary tree with N ≥ 1 total nodes: if N is odd, the count is C_((N-1)/2); if N is even, the count is zero. Every internal node has exactly two children, so I internal nodes imply I+1 leaves and N=2I+1. Left and right children are distinguished; this counts shapes, not arbitrary node labelings.

Quick checks: 4 matrices → C_3=5; a pentagon → C_3=5; 7 total nodes in a full binary tree → C_3=5. A single-node tree corresponds to C_0=1.

notes.title: Catalan Numbers — Formulas and Common Uses
notes.takeaway: C_n = binom(2n,n)/(n+1), with C_0=1. Look for a unique root or matching pair that splits an object into two independent smaller Catalan objects.
notes.details:
FORMULAS
For integer n ≥ 0:
C_n = binom(2n,n)/(n+1) = (2n)! / [n! × (n+1)!].
C_0 = 1. For n ≥ 1: C_n = Σ from k=0 to n-1 of C_k × C_(n-1-k).
Successive values: C_(n+1) = C_n × 2(2n+1)/(n+2).
C_0 through C_7: 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132, 429.

COMMON OBJECTS COUNTED BY C_n
• Well-formed parentheses strings with n pairs, using one bracket type.
• Structurally different BSTs on n fixed, distinct keys. Each shape has one BST-valid labeling; insertion orders are not counted.
• Binary-tree shapes with n nodes, distinguishing left from right, including a left-only child versus a right-only child.
• Full ordered binary-tree shapes with n internal nodes and n+1 leaves: every internal node has exactly two children.
• Full binary parenthesizations of n+1 operands or matrices, preserving their order.
• Triangulations of a convex polygon with n+2 fixed vertices (n ≥ 1).
• Dyck paths with n upward and n downward steps, never below the starting height.
• Noncrossing perfect pairings/handshakes among 2n fixed points around a circle.
• Valid operation sequences containing n stack pushes and n pops, never popping an empty stack.

WHY THE RECURRENCE APPEARS
A unique root or matching pair leaves sizes k and n-1-k. Multiply independent choices for the two parts, then sum over disjoint splits. The decomposition must be complete and unique; a familiar-looking split alone is not a proof.

WATCH OUT
These are common Catalan families, not every possible application. Left/right order, fixed labels/positions, and noncrossing or prefix-validity conditions matter. Full is not the same as complete or perfect. Stack rows count push/pop patterns, not arbitrary permutations of input values. C_0=1 represents an empty or trivial object as appropriate. The factorial formula can overflow even when the final answer fits; use suitable exact arithmetic, and do not perform ordinary division modulo a number without justification. Counting objects is different from generating them: returning C_n strings of length 2n requires Ω(n × C_n) time and output space.

notes.title: Stars and Bars — Count Distributions
notes.takeaway:
• Distribute n identical items among k distinct groups; empty groups allowed.
• Use n stars and k−1 bars → n+k−1 positions.
• Choose bar positions: C(n+k−1, k−1).
• Sorted vowel strings: five vowel counts → C(n+4, 4).
notes.details:
WHEN IT APPLIES
For integers n ≥ 0 and k ≥ 1, count distributions of n identical items among k distinguishable groups, with zero allowed in any group and no extra upper limits. Equivalently, count nonnegative integer solutions of x₁ + x₂ + … + xₖ = n.

WHY THE FORMULA WORKS
Represent the n items by identical stars. Use k−1 bars to separate them into k groups in a fixed order. There are n+k−1 positions altogether. Choose which k−1 positions contain bars; all remaining positions contain stars. Each bar arrangement gives exactly one count distribution, and each count distribution gives exactly one bar arrangement. Therefore the count is C(n+k−1, k−1) = C(n+k−1, n). Adjacent bars, or a bar at either end, represent empty groups.

EXAMPLE: SORTED VOWEL STRINGS
A nondecreasing string using a, e, i, o, u is uniquely determined by its five vowel counts; repetition is allowed. For length n, the counts satisfy a+e+i+o+u=n. Four bars divide n stars into five vowel groups.

** | | | | *
Counts: (2, 0, 0, 0, 1)
String: aau

Thus the count is C(n+4, 4) = (n+1)(n+2)(n+3)(n+4)/24. For n=3, C(7,4)=35.

THE VOWELS ARE NOT IDENTICAL
a, e, i, o, u are five distinct group labels. The stars represent identical, not-yet-labeled units of length to assign among those groups, not five identical vowel types or already-chosen letters. A unit assigned to the a group contributes one a; a unit assigned to the e group contributes one e. We count how many of each vowel to use. Sorted order then gives exactly one string per count vector.

WATCH OUT
• The items are identical; the groups are distinguishable.
• Counts total exactly n.
• The formula above allows zero and assumes no extra upper limits. Requiring every group to be nonempty, imposing upper limits, or changing whether items/groups are distinguishable changes the counting problem; do not reuse the formula unchanged.
• Counts uniquely determine a sorted string, not every unsorted arrangement of its letters.

notes.title: Monotonic Stack: Order vs Scan Direction
notes.takeaway:
• Read stack order bottom→top: [1,3,5] increasing; [5,3,1] decreasing.
• Compare values/heights, not stored indices.
• Ask stack for my answer: previous/left → scan left→right; next/right → scan right→left.
• Use me to answer popped elements: next/right → scan left→right; previous/left → scan right→left.
• Scan direction and stack order are separate choices.
notes.details:
STACK ORDER
In these notes, read stack order from bottom to top using the values being compared. The stack may store indices, but height[st.back()] is the compared value; st.back() is the top index. Strictly increasing excludes equal values; nondecreasing allows them. Strictly decreasing excludes equal values; nonincreasing allows them.

TWO STANDARD PATTERNS
1. Query current: after popping unsuitable candidates, the surviving top answers the current index. Scan left→right for previous/left boundaries and right→left for next/right boundaries.
2. Resolve popped: the current index answers each index it pops. Scan left→right to resolve next/right boundaries and right→left to resolve previous/left boundaries.

These are two standard implementations, not restrictions on every possible algorithm. The traversal determines which side is available; the comparison determines which values remain useful. For a right-to-left resolve-popped previous-smaller search, write left[poppedIndex] = currentIndex, rather than treating the surviving top as a left-side answer for the current index.

POP CONDITIONS — QUERY-CURRENT PATTERN ONLY
• Want top < current: pop while top >= current.
• Want top <= current: pop while top > current.
• Want top > current: pop while top <= current.
• Want top >= current: pop while top < current.
If the stack becomes empty, use the missing-boundary convention required by the problem.

CONNECTION TO LC1504
Previous strictly smaller: scan left→right and pop height[top] >= height[i]; remaining heights are strictly increasing bottom→top.
Next smaller-or-equal: scan right→left and pop height[top] > height[i]; remaining heights are nondecreasing bottom→top.
A forward pop-≥ operation also establishes a next smaller-or-equal boundary for each popped index. The same operation can reveal the current element's previous boundary and resolve another element's next boundary.

WATCH OUT
Do not infer scan direction from the words increasing/decreasing. Say whether the current element receives an answer or supplies answers to popped elements. Do not copy the query-current pop table blindly into resolve-popped code. Equal-value handling depends on the required relation and, for contribution counting, the chosen tie owner.

notes.title: Name Numeric States
notes.takeaway: Use named constants like `RIGHT = 0` and `DOWN = 1`, then write `dir == RIGHT` instead of remembering what `0` and `1` mean.

notes.title: C++ Bitmask Quick Reference
notes.takeaway:
• Count 1s: __builtin_popcount(mask); use __builtin_popcountll for unsigned long long.
• Bit b: test &, set |, clear & ~, toggle ^ with 1ULL << b.
• Unsigned shifts: << k multiplies by 2^k if it fits; >> k divides, rounding down.
• Masks act as sets; bit positions start at 0 from the right.
notes.details:
CONVENTION
Bit positions start at 0 from the right. Unless a different type is stated, assume mask, x, a, and b are 64-bit unsigned long long values. In formulas using a bit position, call it pos. Shift amounts must be integers from 0 through 63. These width-specific rules assume a 64-bit unsigned long long.

COUNTING BITS
• Count 1s in unsigned int → __builtin_popcount(mask)
• Count 1s in unsigned long long → __builtin_popcountll(mask)
• For bitset<N> bits → bits.count()
• Count 0s among the lowest n bits → n − __builtin_popcountll(mask), provided no higher bits are set.
• Use the builtin matching the operand type; plain popcount can lose the high bits of a 64-bit value.

WORKING WITH ONE BIT
• Make only bit pos equal to 1 → 1ULL << pos
• Check bit pos → (mask & (1ULL << pos)) != 0
• Set bit pos to 1 → mask |= (1ULL << pos)
• Clear bit pos to 0 → mask &= ~(1ULL << pos)
• Toggle bit pos → mask ^= (1ULL << pos)
• Include a bit without changing the old mask → newMask = mask | (1ULL << pos)

POWERS OF TWO AND ARITHMETIC
• Calculate 2^k → 1ULL << k
• Multiply unsigned x by 2^k → x << k, if the result fits.
• Divide unsigned x by 2^k, rounding down → x >> k
• Unsigned x % 2^k → x & ((1ULL << k) - 1)
• Check odd → (x & 1ULL) != 0
• ^ means XOR, not exponentiation.
• Unsigned left shifts discard overflowing high bits; they are not exact multiplication once the mathematical result exceeds the type's range.

MASKS AS SETS
• Union → a | b
• Intersection → a & b
• Elements in a, but not b → a & ~b
• Is a a subset of b? → (a & b) == a
• Are they disjoint? → (a & b) == 0
• Lowest n bits all set → full = (1ULL << n) - 1, for 0 ≤ n < 64
• For all 64 bits set, use ~0ULL instead; never shift by 64.
• Flip only those n bits → (~mask) & full
• n items have 2^n possible subset masks, including the empty mask 0. This is a mathematical count; 2^64 itself cannot fit in a 64-bit unsigned integer.

USEFUL EXTRA TRICKS
• Remove the lowest set bit → mask &= (mask - 1)
• Isolate the lowest set bit → mask & -mask, with an unsigned mask.
• Index of the lowest set bit → __builtin_ctzll(mask); mask must be nonzero.
• Exactly one bit set / power of two → mask != 0 && (mask & (mask - 1)) == 0
• The lowest-bit removal/isolation formulas return 0 for an unsigned zero mask. Do not confuse that with ctz: __builtin_ctzll(0) is undefined.

WATCH OUT
• Keep parentheses around bit tests before comparing them, for example (mask & bit) != 0.
• 1ULL gives the shift a wide unsigned left operand; assigning 1 << pos to a wider variable afterward does not widen the original operation.
• Do not transfer these unsigned arithmetic rules blindly to negative signed values.
• The __builtin_* functions are compiler extensions, not portable standard-library function names.

notes.title: Choose the DP State With Simpler Bookkeeping
notes.takeaway: Same time complexity, different bookkeeping. Choose the DP state that makes transitions, base cases, and the final answer easier to express.
notes.details:
State design changes what each stored answer means, not just which direction the loops run. Two correct states can have the same asymptotic time complexity while needing different boundary checks and answer accumulation.

EXAMPLE — OUT OF BOUNDARY PATHS (LC576)
• Remaining-moves state: f(r,c,left) counts ways to exit from this cell within left moves. Outside returns 1; inside with zero moves returns 0. Sum the four neighbors with left−1. The final answer is f(startRow,startColumn,maxMove). Check outside before zero moves so an exit on the final allowed move counts.
• Arrival state: g(steps,r,c) counts ways to reach this inside cell after exactly steps moves, without having exited earlier. Accumulate transitions that leave the grid over moves 1 through maxMove; the last inside layer alone is not the answer. Never continue a path after it exits.

For a positive move budget T, both standard DPs take O(Tmn) time on an m×n grid and can use O(mn) space with rolling bottom-up layers. Their bookkeeping differs even though these bounds match.

WATCH OUT
Choose among correct states that retain enough information and meet the time/space limits. A suffix or remaining-moves state is not universally better; forward tabulation can be simple too. Here the remaining-moves formulation makes the requested exit count direct.

notes.title: Jensen's Inequality — Function of an Average
notes.takeaway:
• Convex f: f(Σ wᵢxᵢ) ≤ Σ wᵢf(xᵢ).
• Weights: wᵢ ≥ 0 and Σ wᵢ = 1.
• Function of weighted average ≤ weighted average of function values.
• Concave f: reverse the inequality.
• Convexity/concavity must hold across the interval containing the inputs.
notes.details:
For real inputs x₁,…,xₙ in an interval where f is convex, and nonnegative weights w₁,…,wₙ summing to 1:
f(Σ wᵢxᵢ) ≤ Σ wᵢf(xᵢ).

The left side averages the inputs first, then applies f. The right side applies f to each input first, then averages those outputs. For a concave function, the inequality reverses.

TWO-POINT FORM
f((1−t)a + tc) ≤ (1−t)f(a) + tf(c), for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1. Geometrically, a convex graph stays on or below the line segment joining two points on it.

CONNECTION TO OUR ABSOLUTE-SUM DISCUSSION
Absolute value is convex. If A ≤ B ≤ C, write B=(1−t)A+tC. Then, for any common added X:
|B+X| ≤ (1−t)|A+X| + t|C+X| ≤ max(|A+X|,|C+X|).
If A=C, all three are equal and the result is immediate.

WATCH OUT
Weights must be nonnegative and sum to 1. Do not apply this inequality to an arbitrary function without establishing convexity or concavity on the relevant interval. Differentiability is not required.

notes.title: Maximum Absolute Subarray Sum — Keep Smallest and Largest Signed Sums
notes.takeaway:
• For maximum absolute subarray sum, keep the smallest and largest signed sums ending here.
• After adding the same future sum, anything between them cannot beat both ends in absolute value.
• Jensen's inequality: |b+x| ≤ max(|a+x|, |c+x|) when a ≤ b ≤ c.
notes.details:
All candidates here are subarrays ending at the same index, so each can take the same future extension x.

If a ≤ b ≤ c, then a+x ≤ b+x ≤ c+x. The middle number cannot be farther from zero than both ends.

JENSEN PROOF
For a<c, write b=(1−t)a+tc with 0≤t≤1. Absolute value is convex, so:
|b+x| ≤ (1−t)|a+x| + t|c+x| ≤ max(|a+x|, |c+x|).
If a=c, all three sums are equal.

DP UPDATE
largest = max(currentValue, oldLargest + currentValue)
smallest = min(currentValue, oldSmallest + currentValue)
answer = max(answer, abs(largest), abs(smallest))

Keep signed sums, not their absolute values. Take the answer over all ending indices, not only the last one. Also allow starting a new subarray at the current element. The proof relies on comparing candidates with the same future choices; it is not a rule for arbitrary DP states.

notes.title: Maximum Subarray — Start Fresh or Extend
notes.takeaway:
• Ending here: max(current number, previous ending sum + current number).
• Previous sum is negative? Leave it and start here.
• Answer = largest ending sum seen anywhere.
• Non-empty subarray: initialize with nums[0], not zero.
notes.details:
Kadane keeps the best sum of a non-empty subarray ending exactly at the current index.

ending = max(nums[i], previousEnding + nums[i])
answer = max(answer, ending)

Why drop a negative previous sum? Adding it only makes the new sum smaller. Starting with nums[i] is better. If the previous sum is zero, starting fresh and extending tie.

Start ending and answer at nums[0]. For [-5, -2], the answer is -2, not 0. In the reset-to-zero version, update the answer before resetting a negative running sum; that zero means carry nothing into the next iteration, not select an empty answer.

Only the previous ending sum is needed: O(n) time and O(1) extra space. This is start-or-extend for a contiguous subarray, not permission to skip an interior element.

notes.title: Jump Game II — Earlier Indices Need No More Jumps
notes.takeaway: Reaching an earlier index never requires more jumps than reaching a later index.
notes.details:
For standard Jump Game, every shorter forward jump up to nums[i] is allowed, and each jump costs one. Let dp[i] be the minimum jumps from index 0 to i. Then a < b implies dp[a] ≤ dp[b] whenever b is reachable.

WHY
Take an optimal path to b. Find the first jump that reaches or passes a. Shorten that jump to land exactly on a, then stop. This uses no more jumps than the path to b. For a = 0, no jumps are needed.

USE IN DP
To reach i, consider reachable predecessors j < i with j + nums[j] ≥ i. The earliest such j has the smallest dp[j] among those candidates, so dp[i] = dp[j] + 1. In a left-to-right predecessor scan, the first valid predecessor is enough; later ones cannot improve the jump count.

WATCH OUT
This is about the minimum jumps needed to reach an index, not its outgoing jump length. It does not say to always land at the earliest index or always take the longest jump. The proof depends on being allowed to shorten a jump and on equal per-jump costs; it need not hold for exact-length jumps, arbitrary graph edges, or differently weighted jumps. LC45 guarantees the last index is reachable; otherwise track unreachable states explicitly.

notes.title: DP — what else can I try?
notes.takeaway:
• State: Would prefix/suffix, index/value, or fewer dimensions simplify it?
• Memoization → tabulation: What order makes dependencies ready?
• Space optimization: Only previous rows needed? Rolling arrays. In-place? Preserve old values before overwriting.
• Circular buffer: Only the last k states needed? Reuse slots after reading their old answers.
• Predecessor search: Can I use the first valid predecessor instead of checking all? Prove it is enough, then check whether a pointer can move only forward without missing future candidates.
• Repeated range sum: Can prefix sums remove the inner loop?
• Sliding-window maximum/minimum: Can a deque, heap, or ordered set maintain it?
• Other range queries: Could a segment tree or a suitable Fenwick tree help?
• Many Boolean states: Could bitsets update several together?
• Greedy alternative: Can I prove a discarded choice will never give a better answer?

These are options to check—not compulsory steps or categories every DP must fit.
notes.details:
Use this checklist after understanding what each state means and which earlier answers it depends on. A different representation must preserve every distinction that affects future choices.

CONDITIONS TO CHECK
• Tabulation needs an order in which the required dependencies are already available. Rolling arrays and in-place updates must preserve every still-needed old value.
• A k-slot circular buffer works only when all needed history fits that window. Read the old slot's answer before reusing it; do not overwrite a dependency while still evaluating candidates.
• Predecessor search: for an existence/Boolean transition, one valid reachable predecessor can be enough. For minimization or maximization, prove the first valid predecessor gives an optimal value. Advance past a candidate only when it is permanently irrelevant, or its finalized DP value proves it cannot help; an uncomputed state is not false. For a moving candidate window, prove its endpoints move only forward and skipped candidates cannot be needed later. This can optimize a DP lookup without making the algorithm greedy.
• Prefix sums help when the repeated transition is a sum over a known range and the contributing values are ready. They do not replace arbitrary range operations.
• A monotonic deque needs a suitably moving window and a dominance argument: a discarded candidate is no better and expires no later than its replacement. Heap or ordered-set versions must remove or ignore expired candidates and handle duplicates correctly.
• Segment trees need a valid merge operation. Fenwick trees support particular operation/update combinations: ordinary range sums can subtract two prefix sums, while min/max variants have additional update restrictions.
• Bitsets help when word-level operations express the Boolean transition; being Boolean alone is not enough. Greedy still needs a proof that discarded alternatives cannot improve the result.

notes.title: Jump Games — rules, goal, DP and shortcut
notes.takeaway:
• I — Reach the last index? Farthest reachable boundary.
• II — Fewest jumps? BFS-style layers.
• VI — Maximum score with jumps 1..k? DP + decreasing deque.
• VII — Reach the last index via zeros, jumps min..max? DP + reachable-window count.
• VIII (in progress) — Minimum landing cost with value-based jump rules; next-greater/equal and next-smaller stack connection to explore.
notes.details:
The shared setting is moving between array positions. The legal jumps and the objective decide the DP—not the name “Jump Game”. For the variants below, jumps go forward, so earlier indices can supply prefix-state transitions.

I — JUMP GAME (LC55)
Rule: from j, any forward distance 1..nums[j] is allowed, within the array. Goal: can we reach n−1?
State: dp[i] = whether i is reachable. Base: dp[0] = true. Transition: OR over reachable j < i with j + nums[j] ≥ i. Answer: dp[n−1].
Shortcut: allowed shorter jumps make the reachable set a prefix. Scan only reachable indices and maintain its farthest boundary: O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
Source: https://leetcode.com/problems/jump-game/description/

II — JUMP GAME II (LC45)
Rule: the same 1..nums[j] forward jumps; reaching the last index is guaranteed. Goal: minimum jump count.
State: dp[i] = minimum jumps to reach i. Base: dp[0] = 0; other entries start at infinity. Transition: 1 + minimum dp[j] among legal predecessors. Answer: dp[n−1].
Shortcut: process the range reached with the current jump count and collect the farthest boundary for the next count. These are BFS-style layers, not a rule to land on the farthest index after every jump. O(n) time, O(1) extra space; n = 1 needs zero jumps.
Source: https://leetcode.com/problems/jump-game-ii/description/

VI — JUMP GAME VI (LC1696)
Rule: jump forward by 1..k. Goal: maximum sum of visited nums values, including index 0 and the last index. k limits one jump's length, not the number of jumps.
State: dp[i] = maximum score ending at i. Base: dp[0] = nums[0]. Transition: dp[i] = nums[i] + max(dp[j]) for max(0,i−k) ≤ j < i. Answer: dp[n−1], not the maximum over every endpoint.
Shortcut: maintain the eligible DP scores in a decreasing deque. Remove expired indices from the front and dominated scores from the back. Order by dp values, not raw nums values. Each index enters and leaves at most once, giving O(n) time.
Source: https://leetcode.com/problems/jump-game-vi/description/

VII — JUMP GAME VII (LC1871)
Rule: jump forward by minJump..maxJump and land only on a '0'. The start is '0'. Goal: reach the last index.
State: dp[i] = whether i is reachable. Base: dp[0] = true. For i > 0, eligible predecessors lie in [max(0,i−maxJump), i−minJump]; a negative upper endpoint means no predecessors. dp[i] is true only if s[i] is '0' and that window contains a true state. Answer: dp[n−1].
Shortcut: maintain the count of reachable predecessors as the window moves. Add dp[i−minJump] when in bounds; remove dp[i−maxJump−1] when in bounds. A positive count supplies the OR result in O(1) per index, O(n) total. Zero landing cells and a minimum jump length can create gaps, so one farthest boundary alone is insufficient.
Source: https://leetcode.com/problems/jump-game-vii/description/

VIII — JUMP GAME VIII (LC2297): IN PROGRESS
For i < j, a legal jump satisfies either:
• nums[j] ≥ nums[i], with every intermediate value < nums[i]; or
• nums[j] < nums[i], with every intermediate value ≥ nums[i].
Pay costs[j] when landing; starting at index 0 is free. Goal: minimum cost to reach n−1.
Proposed prefix state, not yet worked through together: dp[i] = minimum landing cost to reach i. Base: dp[0] = 0, others infinity. Candidate transition: costs[i] + minimum dp[j] over legal predecessors j. Intended answer: dp[n−1].
Connection to explore: the next greater-or-equal and next strictly smaller positions to the right, found with monotonic stacks. Only the rules and this hint have been discussed; the DP derivation and implementation are not marked complete.
Source: https://algo.monster/liteproblems/2297

KEEP THIS COMPARISON OPEN
I, II, VI and VII have been covered in the study discussion. Add other variants as they are studied; this card makes no claims about III, IV, V or IX. Similar names do not justify reusing a shortcut without checking its assumptions.
